A SCHEME FOIL A HIGHLAND LAND Tuner, to decide I upon rent and other matters of dispute between lairds and crofters, to enable-the latter to purchase their hold- ings, and to provide fo,r the] enlargement ofamall hold- ings, has been issued by Mr. D. F. C. Shearer, F.P.,Caith- ness-shire. It is good as far sa It 'goes, except for the danger of sub-division, -and for the fact that 25 years' purchase is too much to pay for the restoration of lands stolen from the clans by the predecessors of the present owners. In addition, the three F's chould be seevred to crofters who do not desire to purchase, and there should be &provision against sub-letting and sub-divisiont. If the crofters had the three F's they would not need to purchase their holdings. In a csrcular accompanying the scheme Mr. Shearer says :—" I know a farm held by a man on a short lease, during which he nearly rebut the farmhouse, fenced and drained the had, and re- claimed a considerable quantity in addition; and I know tthat on applying for a renewal at a reasonable advance, te was told that his rent was to be nearly doubled,and g he did not choose to take it on these terms, another man w-suld. He remonstrated with the factor, stating that he had made the place what it was by his labour and outlay, but it was no use, the farm was actually let to another man and this industrious man had to leave the farm he had made what it was 'without receiving a penny of compensation for what had become worth to the proprietor over six hundred pounds. Whatever this may be called by some people, I call it robbery." Mr. Shearer also points out other abuses, and declares that the con- dition of things on a largo estate in Caithness is a dis- grace to civilisation. RENT REDUCTION.—The NarklaneExpress gives a table showing the gross rental of farms, market gardens, and nurseries (schedule B) in England and Scotland sepa- rately and together for 1852-3, 1879-80, and 1882-3, with the increase that took place between the first and second of these years, and the decrease between the second and third :

England & Wales. Scotland. Gt 'Britain. 1852-3 1879-80 1882-3 Increase 52-3 to 79-80 10,468,347 Decrease 79-80 to 82-3 3,356,568 Nearly all the great increase of rental occurred in twenty years, between 1856 and 1876. Major Cragie remarks in the Standard on the greater increase in other kinds of in- come during the period of inflation, but that is quite ir- relevant to the question. Our object is to show that a substantial reduction of rents in England and Scotland is essential to prevent land from going out of cultivation to a very alarming extent. Instead of being higher than in 1853, as they are, rents should be lower, as land is certainly worth less to farm now than it was then. At the former period there was no reason to _fear such prices for corn as now prevail, and, as a matter of fact, high or moderate prices followed, 1853 for many years. Now, on the contrary, it is almost a certainty -that low prices will prevail for many years to come, though not, we trust, quite such extremely low prices as are current to-day. An apt illustration of the depression was seen at a sale in Devon a few days since, when an estate of 420 acres was sold for a little over £B,OOO, whereas some few years since the sum of £lB,OOO was refused for the same estate. _

A Crowd gathered round, and, of course, took part with the ;luly, and true it was the lady's leg had been pinched by her fellow traveller, but not the imfeathered biped whom she suspected. The guard drew from under her seat a I basket containing alive goose—the sinner whose assaults had galvanised the lady into indignation against the gentleman. Loud was the laughter of the bystanders; and plaintiff and defendant reiumed their journey to Southport in mutual good humour—the irmer ad- monished by the incident against hasty conclusions. , TEACUP LORE.—Pictures in a teacup? Well, the idea is not altogether a new one, and many of my little friends have, no doubt, tried the old-fe-shioned plan of making pictures, or, as I think it is called, "telling fo tunes,' in a teacup. In fact, I have a friend who IS quite renowned for her success as a fortune-teller through her 'skill in shaking and tapping a teacup until the vounds, or tea-leaves, in the bottom .of the teacup assume, in a rude way, certain shapes ae forms repre- senting people, animals, and various otherkaages which she professes to understand as referring ictoome way to the person whose fortune she happens to beitelling at the time. I was present once when she told, in this way, the fortune of a young lady. The prophecy and the method of making it seemed to mete be very vague; but the gist of it all was,-that in a short time a young gentleman of extremely prepossessing appearance would arrive, and that he was,in.some unexplained way, to exert a powerful Influence on the future prospects of the youiv lady. Wishing to discover what there was in the cup to arrant such a forecast, I obtained possession of it withoutbeing observed. In the bottom of the nap I saw that the tea- leaves had assumed a form which, with a little aid of the imagination, migott be accepted ais resembling a wry spare, delicate, and altogether dilapidated young men. With the aid of a teaspoon, and using a few other grounds or leaves that were lying on the bottom of the cup, I quickly chaii,ged the young man into a most dis- reputable looking old tramp, with a bie bundle on his back, and accompanied by a ferocious-looking Wilde.% Then I waited the result,. Presently, the young lei whose fortune had been foretold took up the cup, wit a blush of pleasure, to examine its contents. The mo- ment she saw the dreadful figure ef the old tramp, she exclaimed, "What a horrid old fright !" Then there was a great commotion, which was only quelled when I acknowledged my guilt. But I had learned something, which was that, with a little management, and a tea- spoon, pictures of many kinds could be made in a tea. cup.—C. C. Ward, in St. IVicholas. SCOTCHMEN AND Samoa Music. —A gentleman who was a first-rate performer of Scotch music on the violin spent a winter at 'Exeter, and, of course, soon became acquainted with the mnsical dilettanti. of the place. truing one day with a professor, the conversation turned upon Scotch music, and a strong argument arose as to its bearing competition with foreign music. The Scotch- man, whom we shall for the moment designate the Fiddler, insisted that, when properly played, nothing could excel it; the Professor, on the other hand, insist- ing that it was only fit for the barnyard.—" I'll tell you what," says the Fiddler, "I'll lay you a bet of £5 that if a party of Scotchmen can be got together I'll make them shed tears one minute, sing the next, and dance the tkird."—" D one," says the Professor, "And if your music is capable of that I will not only pay the £5 with plea- sure, but will be convinced that it is the most enliven- ing, pathetic, and best music in the world."—The diffi- culty arose as to getting an opportunity for a trial. But, being infOrmed that a number of young Seotchmen wore to dine at a certain London hotel on the anniver- sary of Burns's birthday, it was agreed to pay them a visit. It was considered a capital opportunity by the Fiddler, for these young, men being principally raw- boned, overgrown Scotch lads, who had recently left their own country to carry tea in the neighbourhood, were the very ones upon whom he was sure to make a hit. All being now arranged, and the utmost secrecy being agreed upon, the eventful day was anxiously looked for. At length it cattle, and the Fiddier and the Professor, by an introduction to one of the party, got an invitation to the dinner. There were twelve altogether sat down, and a right merry party they soon became, for the whisky toddy was not spared when the memory of any of Scotia's bards was proposed. The Fiddler was not long in perceiving that he had got among a right musical set, and he waited patiently till they were in that happy state when they were fit for anything. At length he gave a wink to the Professor, who at once pro- posed that his friend should favour them with a Scotch tune on the violin.—" Capital, capital!" cried the whole party.—The violin was brought, and all were in breath- less anxiety. The Fiddler chose for hisfirst tune "Here's a health to them that's awa'," and played it in the most solemn and pathetic manner.—" That's a wofu' tune," said a great, big, raw-boned youth to his next neighbour. —"lt is that, Sandy. There's mickle in that tune, man. It reminds me o' ane that's gene ; " Jamie at the same time giving a deep sigh and drawing his hand over his long, gaunt face to hide the tears which were trickling down his cheeks. The Fiddler with his keen eye soon perceived that before he got through the second part of the tune he would have them all in the same mood. He therefore threw his whole soul into the instrument, played the tune as he had never done before, and, as the last four bars of the tune died away-like the distant echo, there was not a dry cheek amongst the company. Now is the time, thought the Fiddler, and without stopping a moment struck up, in a bold, vigorous style, "Willie brew'd a peck o' maut." In went the handkerchiefs, away Tent the tears. " Chorus !" cried the Fiddler, and in an instant all struck up— For we are nae feu, we're nae that fou. ku RASICBERRY is one of the moSt profitable of,Eng,, fruits., Its late flowering habit places it beyond the reach of severe Spring frosts, which prove so disastrous to other fruits, so that the crop seldorn fails, neither does ' the price vary. In exceptionally dry seasons, on light or sandy soil, the crop may be diminished, but no one should plant the raspberry extensively in slid' a posi- tion. The most suitable is a clamp and moderately, heavy loam. In clayey soil they do not thrive unless it has been well draided and cultivated, and made rich with manure. It is seldom that raspberry plants require renewing, as they can be annually invigorated by the application of heavy top dressing with manure, a sys- tem of culture that suits admirably a surface reciting plant like the raspberry. It would, at the same- time, in many instances be economy to Uproot some of the old small growing varieties, and replace them with Carter's prolific Prince of Wales,-or Fastolf. The land for new plantations should be trenched and manurea two feet deep, and the planting may be done from the end oI Oct. to the time they are about starting in the 'Spring. The I distance between the rows may be four or five feet, and the plants in the row may be from one to three feet, ac- ' 'cording to the adopted system of training, and the greater distance should have three plants, forming an equilateral triangle, with an iron or wooden support in the centre. Another method of supporting them is to bring two lots together and tie their ends to form an arch, which seems to answer the purpose iii. sheltered localities. When the plants are only a foot distant they form a continuous rove, and the method of supporting must be the same, which may consist of wire stretched and attached to posts, or narrow battens ,may be fixed to upright posts driven into the ground, to which the canes may be secured. The majority of canes will not require supportit.ig, the first year, as they are generally cut down to six inches from the base. Large growers of this fruit use no supports whatever, but simply run a piece of string loosely round the canes, which they shorten to about three feet, so that the wind may not have so much power over them. The wood of the rasp- berry that bears fruit is of ne further use, and must be annually removed, which we endeavour to do in frosty weather, as the ground is then hard underfoot. - The

tops of the canes-that are intended to fruit next year are taken off, so as to reduce their height to about five feet; they are then tied to their supports. After the prunings are collected we make a practice of covering the surface of the ground two or three filches deep with the best manure that can be got. In small gardens a row of raspberry canes may be planted near the path and run- ing 411 the same direction, and-trained to a continuous support.

The toPs' of many plants-will have been destroyed by the frost, and it will be neces- sary to move thena so as to give the beds or borders a neat appearance. All newly-planted rose trees" should have the soil pressed down wound their roots, as the frost has a tendency to loosen the soil. They should also receive what gardeners berm mulching, by which is Meant that the ground should be covered round the plants to, a depth of six inches with half-decayed manure, which will protect the roots from vicissitudes of temperature as well as preventing-the upheaVing of soil by the frost. I venture to say that with a sufficient knowledge of the best out-of-door varieties of Chrysanthemums the hardy flower garden may be as bright now (November 22nd) as.any time of the year. THE PROPOSED TAX ON BACHELORS; • OR, SMILER'S STRATAGE BY J. &ATM A few weeks after our friend Smiler's memorable keesunin' dooment," Ise was seated one evening by the side of a well-tilled table, busily engaged, in company with his wife, in the pleasant occupation of partaking of tea and toast, it being their usual " baggin' " hour. Smiler had a newspaper by his side, from which he, at intervals, read the incident of the day. Suddenly his eye, fell upon the following paragraph : " PROPOSED TAX ON BATCHELORS. "The Paris correspondent of the Globe writes ;--' There is one item in the programme of the next session upon which the financiers and stockbrokers may have based their calculations. It is seriously proposed to levy a tax on bachelors.' " 0 Well, if ever aw yeard owt like that afore!" exclaimed our hero; " an' yet it's noun a bad idea, 'loather. Betty," to his wife, who, I must here premise, had net recovered her "hearing," "wot doesta think thur beaten t' do ie France?" " Wot's that theau says, Smiler," said Betty, glaring savagely at her liege lord, "abeaut a atink? it's thi nose, moo, ut's getten eaut o' order; thur's no smell here 'cept wot theau may ha' browt fro' th' Owd Heause a-Wham." "Aw didno' say owt o'th' sooart, Bette," yelled Smiler, nearly dislocating his jaws in the effort he made to make himself heard. " Wot aw wantud t' tell thi war ut th' pepper here says ut th' French Government intend to put a tax on bachilors—male an' faymale—if thi dunno mak' it up an' get wed; but thoau'rt so danged deeaf, Betty, thur s no ruakkin' thi yer one." "Poor wench, an' is hoo deead then ?" said Betty, a tetr of sympathy dimming the brightness of her eves. "Aw thowt when aw seed her t' other wick ut hoo're not lung for this wold." " Wot th' duel is th' woman tawkin' abeaut ?" groaned Smiler. "Betty, aw said nowt abeaut onybody bein' deead —aw slid summut quite differunt." " Dee'd beaut givin' a grunt, did boo, poor thing ?" queried Betty, innocently. Smiler, in despair, gave up the fruitless attempt to make his wife comprehend the meaning Pushing the paper over to her, he pointed with his finger to the paragraph, having reference to the proposed bachelor. tax. Betty, having spelled her way carefully through it, severely said: " An' is that wot theau's bin tellin' ml abeaut just neaw, Smiler ?" Our hero nodded by way of answer. "Why, aw tbowt theau're tellin ml ut owd Jacky Brad- shaw's wench wur deend. Ate do raley wish, Smiler, ut when theau speyks, theau'd ger off that nasty habit o' chew- ing thi words. Aw'd ha' one or two o' thoose front teeth poo'd eaut, if aw war thee, an' then thi veyce ad slip eaut o' thi meauth that mich yezzier. An' so thur intendiu' t' mak' ba.chilors oather get wed or bi taxed, are thi? an' quite reet, too. If aw'd ml way, aw'd mak aw owd maids an' bachilors pay so mich, t' help t' support thoose folks at han getten moor childre than they con wed l provide for. Neaw, thures owd Jack-o'-Thimble, a chap ut's noather wife nor chilt t' trouble him; why shudno' he be made t' marry owd Sally Dickson, or else pay summut eout o' his wages t' thoose ut are marred an' badly Nl' need o' help ?" "By George, Betty!" exclaimed our hero, theau's put some mischievous thowts ml yed nt wurn't theer afore," and leaning baok in his chair he gave vent to a hearty beret of laughter. " Wot's up neaw, Smiler ?" haid his wife; "come mak' o' mischief, melt lee.ban." But beyond shouting that "he're nohbut hail& at his thowts, an' not at her," he declined to inform her of the cause of his hilarity, which was nothing more or leas than c -scheme, by which he hoped to induce the above-mentioned Jack-o'-Thimble and Sally Dickson to make a match of it. Having by this time finiahed his tea, Smiler betook himself to the residence ef one of his com- panions, yclopt "Snig.Philip," and soon the two worthies were busily engaged in decising ways and means to carry out a plot which, as the sequel will .show, hilly bore out the old truism that " well that ends well." It so happened that Saig Philip's brother had come on a few days' visit, and when he was informed by his brother and Smiler conjointly that they wished him to become a .party to their little plot, he, after the nature of the business had been fully explained to him, enteced into the spirit of the affair with great gusto. A few days after the above occurrence took place, Snig Philip's brother presented himself at the doer of owd oaelt-oeThirnble. Giving a loud imperious knock which had the desired effect of bringing the wondering Jack to the door in no very gentle mood, Philip's brother somewhat haughtily said: " Whet'e your name, my good follow ?" " Wot's that to thee, aw shod like le know?" "Come,, my men, none of your insolence to me, or I shall be under the painful necessity of having you consigned to the nearest lockup." " Whoa are yo, then, an' what dun yo want ?" I want your name." "John 'thimble, better known as 'Jack-o'-Thimble.'" Oh! Are you married or single?" " Sengle ; an' likely for Win' if that's on'y satisfaction t' yo." "Bow long have you been single, Mr. Thimble ?" "Why, ever sin aw begun o livin bi misel, theau gawby," Bald Jack, now rapidly losing patience. " Insolent again, my man; but under the rather ex- ceptional circumstances I shall let it pass. Well, have you heard of the new law which has come into effect respecting bachelors F' " Naw ; what is it?" "Why, that all bachelors are to be taxed—made to pay so much per head, according to income—for the privilege of being allowed to remain single, or failing that, to get mar- ried within the space of a fortnight from this date. " Well, if ever aw yerd owt like that afore! Hen things room t' etch a pass, then, at th' Government are forced t' mak chaps pay for not gettin' wed? Ate reckon owd maids 'll bi served th' same sauce?" " Certainly. Here [sanding Jack a legal-looking docu- ment] is the paper you will be required to fill up at your earliest opportunity." With that the stranger bade Jack good-day, leaving him in a very disturbed state of mind indeed. No sooner had Philip's brother left the " fowt " behind him than with a loud guffaw he exclaimed: "What a sell for the old chap—swallowed the bait like a htnegry trout !" Soon the pseudo tax-gatherer was wending his way in the direction of Sally Dickson's rose-embowered cottage, which was situated about half-a-mile from Jack-e-Thimble's residence. Arriving at the cottage, Philip's brother knocked at the door, which was promptly opened by Bally, who no sooner caught sight of the stranger's countenance, coupled with the papers he had in his hand, than in trembling ac- coati of terror she exclaimed: "Eh, goodness gracious days elite! wotever's t' do neaw ? Aw've never done nowt wrung, ate know, an' aw never owed any rent i' ml life." "My good woman," said the stranger, "you needn't be afraid; it's only a paper I've brought you, informing you that according to the new law you mast either get married within the space of one month from now, or subject yourself to the tax which is about to be imposed on all maids and bachelors." " Wot's that yo sen ?" cried Sally, her courage now re- turning; "gooin' t' tax owd maids and bachilors ? an' done you yo co that a reet thing t' do? Chonce is a fine thing. Ate reckon if a woman conno' get nob'dy t' ax her hoo'll ha' t' pay th' tax?" "I suppose so," said the stranger, with a smile. "Now, my good woman," continued he, "I've got no time to waste here, so be kind enough to tell me the following particulars : What is your name?" "Sarah Dickson, sur." " Where do you live?" "Here, theau gawby ; conno' theau see that beaut axin' sich a foolish question?" "How old are you?" " Wot done you want t' know that for?" "It is necessary in order that we may have a correct idea of the ages of all the unmarried women in Lancashire." " Well" (scratching her head cogitatatively the while), "aw're but very yang when aw're born. New let ml see; aw're abeawt twenty yer owd when ml fayther dee'd, an' as that is twenty-five yer sin, aw reckon awa't not bi far wrung it aw let yo' put ml deawn—say tharty-five; ten yer 'll mak no difference t' anybody but miser." "Now, Miss Dickson, be very careful what answers you make ; remember that what you say falsely will be used as evidence against you in the future. The stranger having booked the above said, "I will now bid you good evening, Miss."
"Well (hesitatingly), aw'd sich like thowts misel' ; but they sen, theaw knows, Jack, ut it's manners t' wait till yo'r axt."

" Well, aw ax thi neaw; wilta marry mi ? ' "Aw dunce' care if aw do, Jack. Theaw's wantud so neb'dy t' look Other thi a greight while neaw, aw con tell th , owd lad. Mony a time aw've felt sorry for thi, livin' aw alone i' that heawse o' thine, an' heaw nice an' com- fortable theaw met bi wi' a wife like me t' tak care on thi. As fur misel, Jack, it's bin mi own fawt at aw'm a sengle woman. If aw'd had a mind aw met ha' had Billy Jump, Dicky Rump, an' a lot o' others at aw conno' just misre- member neaw; but aw'd made up mi mind at if ever aw gest wed aw'd ha' sotneb'dy as ad keep me, not rue t' keep their, an' so aw towd um t' gooa abeawt their business—an' thi went."

" It seeum3 t' me, Sally," said Jack, " ut fate men t thi for me, an' so th' sooner wi' tnak'n it up th' betther it'll bi for boath on us—not t' mention dooin' th' Government eawt o' Out rascally tax ut thin intendia' t' put on sich as thee an' me."
" Aw'st bi ready when theaw likes t' fotch mi," said Sally, looking slyly at Jack, who sat rather nervously twist- kg his hat in his hands.

" IVell, Sally, aw'll get th' axins put in, an' we'll get married as soon as wi con, so as t' do th' Government eawt o' that rascally tax thur intended t' put on Baden as thee an' me," said Jack, preparing to take his leave. "Good fleet, owd wench,' and (kissing the blushing maid) left her with the pleasant consciousness thrilling his bosom of having been the means of making ona woman at least _

, VVell, to make a long story short, Jack and Sally were married at the old Parish Church on the hill. Mr. and Mrs. Snig Philip and his brother, Billy Yawhaw, and others, and a right marry time was spent. Many a quiet chuckle hid Smiler and his companions over the happy consummation of their little plot, and when, later on in the evening, Smiler told Jack the whole affair, he, Jack, mag- nanimously forgave him, at the same time remarking that " here satisfied wi' his bargain, for neaw he'd ha' someb'dy t' cook his meyls for him i'stead o' being compelled, a 3 before, t' put up wi' mak-shift dinners."—Front Be,t Brierley's Journal.

CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETING. SPEECH. BY SIR &MUM' GREENALL. Oa Monday evening a meeting of the Conservative electors of the south-west ward was held in the Conservative Club. There was a small attendance. The chair was occupied lw Mr. R. Pierpoint, and there were also present Sir Gilbert Greenall, Captain Reynolds, Alderman Webster, Messrs R. J. Wynne Jones, W. D. Jeans, H. Greenall, J. V. Taylor, W. Grica, G. Cropper, John Roberts, Councillor Wright, L. R. Jones, J. L. Wilsm, W. Bonnet, James Westwell, Major G. Bolt-n, and others. The ward officials having been elected,

Mr. BENNET moved " That this meeting pledges itself to use every legitini.,te means in its power to return Sir Gil- bert Greenall, Bart., the chosen and well-tried candidate of the Conservative party, to Parliament as representative for Warrington at the next general election?' (Cheers.) Sir Gilbert Greenall was, Mr. Bennet went on to say, as the resolution said, the well-tried friend of the Conservative party. He was well-tried in many ways. He had served them in more ways than one, and he was prepared to serve them well in the future if they stuck by him and returned him as their representative in the next Parliament. hir Gilbert was a fit and proper candidate, because for one reason, he had the time at his disposal, and for another, he had the means. Some people would tell them that Sir Gil- bert was getting advanced in years, but they found in ancient history and biblical hisrory that the oldest men were always chosen for the most responsible positions. It was always understood that with age came experience and wisdom. They had another proof of Sir Gilbert's ability in the way that he had managed his own business, as when a man could represent his own interests well it showed he was qualified to represent the interests of others. Another reason tor supporting Sir Gilbert was that they knew, his principles and they knew that he would be true to those principles. (Cheers). Mr. J. RonErt-rs, in seconding the resolution, said be had heard said that Sir Gilbert was getting too old to represent the town of Warrington in tho House of Commons, but he (Mr. Roberts) was sure that they had men in the House of Commons as old as Sir Gilbert, and he thought they could rest assured that if Sir Gilbert was in Parliament he would do his duty there in a mincer that would neither disgrace himself nor the borough of Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. Tave.on, in eupporting the resolution, said that he himself thought that alter Sir Gilbart bad respresented War- rington so long it would certainly not be a grateful thing on the part of the el,ctors if they were to desert him at the last moment. (Hear, bear.) Referring to what be termed the ridiculous arernpt to show that Sir Gilbert Greenall was opposed to the abilition of flogging in the army, Mr. Taylor said he happened to hive a few notes in which he found seine reference to flogging. He found that in the Parlitment for 1877, the hon. member for Leicester moved that flogging in the navy be abolished, and be found that Messrs. Gladstone, Hartington, Harcourt, Forster, and Goschen voted against tkat resolution. Therefore he (Mr. Taylor) thought it was rieieulous to raise that outcry against Sir Gilbert, for they would find that the leading men in the Liberal party had done as Sir Gilbert had done. (Ap- plause.) . . -

The resolution was then carried by acclamation, Sir GILBERT GREENALL in responding, acrid : Mr. Pier- point and gentlemen, I will first say Mr. Pierpoint that I and all who are present are very glad indeed to see you here upon this OCCSSit n. We think ourselves fortunate, and we think you, Mr. Pierpoint, also fortunate—we think it no small advantage to Mr. Pierpoint that he lives so near to us as to be able to enter this spacious and good building and to say that he with you and me rejoices to come here. We are all partners in the property, and also in the sentiments which Conservatism contains, and that Con- servatism eas the principle that produced this building. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Bennet, lam most grateful to you. You spoke directly to the substance of the resolution YOU moved. lam greatly obliged to you and to Mr. Robert!. Mr. Roberts has been always right; Mr. Roberts is a man who has never made any mistake, and when he speaks favourably of men I am almost disposed think better of myself than I should have done if I had not had not had Mr. Roberts' good opinion and good word. I am very much obliged to you and to my friend Mr. Taylor. Ile has spoken most kindly. I have heard Mr. Taylor speak before. I like to hear Mr. Taylor speak, because he always speaks to say something. There are a great many speakers who rise to utter words and really an I truly say nothing. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) And now with respect to my- self, I do not ask you to say " pity the sorrows of a poor old lean." (Loud lauebter.) Ido not ask you to say that. I would be grateful and thank God for the measure of health and strength which he gives me. I speak plainly. I may be, possibly, in the opinion of many an old person, but in my own opinion—and the gratefulness which I would express towards my Maker for the health he gives—l do not think that in health and strength lam unequal to represent this borough. Believe me and think me and you won't do me an injustice; believe me and think me upside down, or in any shape; believe me and trust me to be a straightforward fel- low. (Cheers and laughter.) And I say this: That if I felt that from infirmity of years I was not fit or able to represent this town I would not have the sentiment of in- justice to you to attempt to represent it. (Hear, hear.) Let us have plain and straightforward intercourse when we meet to- gether. I have not a sentiment or an opinion which I hesi- tate to express; I hate not a sentiment or a feeling which would not alletw me to enter into the most familiar and most straightforward intercourse with any of my fellow creatures in this town. I come before those with whom I am ac- quainted believing that they trust me and the opinions that I hold, and the integrity with which I hold and, I hope, maintain them. I believe that we are not merely political friends, but really and sincerely friends to each other. (Hear, hear.) And now, gentlemen, with respect to our meeting this night, I feel that we only have a small atten- dance; we have, I admit, a small attendance in one respect but a sufficiently large attendance in another res- pect. We are here for business, no political attraction was put forth to bring us together. We wanted to appoint our working committee and our friends; we want a body of volunteers; we want a body of men of principle, straight- forwardness, and political integrity; we intend to work to- gether as true and constitutional Englishmen. We will have no such manceuvres as refreshment houses ; we will hove no such manceavres as attract the stomach and neglect the brains and the head—(laughter)—but we will go right on to the maintenance of the Constitution, the thing which we love; we will go right on to the maintenance of every man who possesses freedom, straightforwardness, the power of expressing his opinions, and we will go right on to say that we know the faith that is in us, and we intend io show by our conduct that we venerate our Constitution, that we love our sovereign, and that we will stand by the integrity of the kingdom. (Cheers.) Captain REYNOLDS, in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman, said he was very pleased to see Mr. Peerpoint in the chair. In some future day when they had established Conservatism again in Parliament, they thought it possible that their chairman would be one of the men they should consider entitled to the priveleee or the honour of being in Parliament. (Cheers.) Councillor WRIGHT seconded the vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was cerdially carried.

"Gad neet, mestur," said Sally. Entering the house Sally muttered "This byets owt ut aw ever yard afore! A poor lone woman like misel' conno' be laft alone i' pace, but man be tax't becose aw'm wot they co'en a splinter—aw meean a spinster. It's noan a reet thing t' do. If aw'd ever thowt ut slob a state o' things nd ha' come'n, aw'd not ha' letten o th' chances tit aw've had-- an' gud tins too—goo-a by—that aw wouldn't. A nice tiring t' tax a faymale when boo's getten welly past th' marryin' age. Heawever (brightening up), aw'm as pratty as owd Jack-o'-Thimble, an' aw'm as sartin o' gerrin a hue- band as he con be a-gettin' a wife." A day or two passed by, Smiler, and those of his com- panions, not to mention Snig Philip's brother, anxiously awaiting he denouenzent of the plot which so far had been succesesfully carried out. ' One afternoon as Sally Dickson was busily engaged doing her household work, who should enter, looking awfully woe- be-gone, but Jack-o'-Thimble. "Afternoon, Sally," said Jack, .seating himself, albeit uninvited, on the nearest chair, without perceiving a pin- cushion which Sally had placed there and forgotten. With a yell of pain Jack sprang up, and expressing himself in a surprising amount of strong language, gently drew a needle from the hinder part of his unmentionables. "Aw reckon theitert wonderin' wot's browt ml here, Sally ?" queried Jack, costing sheepish glances at the ancient maid the while,

A TRAIN WRECK R CALGHT.—A large sleeper was found on Monday lying across the rails near Whitstable, just before the Itarnagate train was due. Inquiries led to the arrest of a farm labnarer named Hudson, who confessed his guilt. Moore gives the story of a man asking a servant, "Is your master at home?" "No sir; he's out." "Your mistress ?" FUrNDERING Or A STEAMER OFF HOLTTERAD. A steamer, which it is almost certain was the Pochard, be- longing to the Cork Steamship Company, sank off Holy. head during a strong, south-westerly gale on Sundtv. The Pochard was of 1,800 tons hurthen, classed Al, commanded by Captain Miller, traded between London, Liverpool, and Rotterdam, and carried a crew of 24. Persons who wit- nessed the vessel founder, expressed the opinion that there was no time to launch a beat, nor was it possible that any one on board could have escaped. The Holyhead lifeboat went out promptly, but was unable to render any assistance.

" FIRE WATERS" ON TRH COYOO —Lord Granville re. c:ived a deputation, on Tuesday, f om the United Kingdom All;ance and the National Temperance League, urging him to snpport the proposition made by Italy, at the Berlin Con- ference, for the exclusion of alcoholic liquors from the Cango basin, where their introduction would paralyse trade and demcraliae and destroy the native population. Canon Ellison, Dr. Byres, Mr. Raper, and Mr. John Taylor sup- ported the object Of the deputation ; and Lord Granville, in reply, said that instructions had been sent to our representa • fives is accordance with the views of the deputation, which would continue to have his warm support, as he felt the importance of protecting the native races from the injurious and fatal effects of the traffic in alcohol.

BINTARESDOROUGII ELECTION—Whit Will p^obably be the last election for the doomed hero u,th of Knaresborough took place on Tuesday, to fill up the vacancy caased by the death of Mr. Tom Collins (C). The caudidates were Col. Gunter (C) and Mr. Angus Holden (L). Polling was fairly heavy considering the smallness of the constituency, and vehicles were freely lent on both sides. As it wae known the majority, whichever won, could not be large' there was plenty of excitement, but everything passed off good humouredly. The result was declared thus i—Ganter (C) 319, Heiden (L) 267, rnijority 52. There were 728 re- gistered electors. In 1881, after ten months' d:sfranclaise- ment, following the unseating of Sir H. PARENTS THE BEST TEACHERS.—There should, indeed, be no better teachers than the father and mother. On them lies the first responsibility towards young souls. It is very well and creditable ,that they should take pains to provide them with Sunday clothes, but how about the Sunday spirit, which should be the spirit of the week? How about the care lest they should offend any of these little ones by their:own carelessness, and outward indifference to religion and Divine worship? What, I repeat, do they expect to follow by sending their children to church if they'd() not go themselves? What good do they think will attend the Sunday lesson to live a godly life, unless they are plainly striving to lead godly lives themselves? Children are guided by example far more than by precopt,by life more than by , lessons, by steady home influence more than; by any ' school discipline.—The Rev. llariv Jones, M.A., in • The I Quiver" for Decenzber. SENTENCE ON THE MIGNONETTE SURVIVORS Thomas Dudley, captain, and Edwin Stephens, mate of the yacht !Mignonette, were on Tuesday brought up before five judges, in the Queen's Bench, for judgment. The court was densely I crowded. 'rho Lord Chief Justice, in passing sentence of ' death on both prisoners, said there was no justifiable homi- cide except in self-defence. In this case the weakest, youngest, and most unresisting was chosen. Was it mere necessary to kill him than One of the grown men? No. It was plainly a case in which the only course was to leave it to the Sovereign to exercise her prerogltive of mercy. Com- ; mitting murder to pteserve one's life could not be held as justification. To preserve one's life was a duty, but the highest duty often required one to sacrifice his life. Dud. Icy pleaded for mercy in a low tone, and Stephens did like- ! wise in broken sentences. The judge stated that he con. curred in the recommendation to mercy made by the jury. We understand that the Secretary of State for the Horne ; Department has advised the Queen to respite the capital ; sentence passed until further signification of her Majesty's pleasure. • CHLORO-LINSEED COUGH LOZ RNGES, a medicated linseed ex- tract, 6d ; p,stage 2d.—Kay Bros , Stockport, and all , CLemists.—Adrt.

Grandpapa's hair is very white, And grandpapa walks but slow; Ho likes to sit still in his easy chair, While the children come and go. "Hush play," quietly says mamma; Let nobody trouble dear grandpa Pa." Grandpapa's hand is thin and weak, It has worked hard all his days; A strong right hand, and an honest hand, That has won all good men's praise. Kiss it tenderly," says nap.mma ; Let evey one honour grandpapa." Grandpapa's eyes are growing dim; They have looked on sorrow and death, But the love-light never went out of them, Nor the courage and the faith. You children, all of you," says mamma, Have need to look up to dear grandpapa." Grandpapa's years are wearing;few, But he leaves a blessing behind; ' A good life lived, and a good fight fought. True heart and equal mind: "Remember, my children," says mamma. "You bear the name of your grandpapa." *--Leeds Mercury Weekly.

A DEAD MARCH. Play me a march low-toned and slow, a march for a silent tread, Fit for the wandering feet of one who dreams of the
silent dead, Lonely—between the bones below and the souls that are overhead. _ . .
Here for awhile they smilei and sang, alive in the inter-
space; Efere with the grass beneath the feet and the stars above _
the face: Now are their_ feet beneath the grass, and whither has
flown their grace? Who shall assure us whence they come, or tell us the
way they go? Verily life with them was joy, and now they hare left us, - - -

Woe; Once they were not, and now they are not; and this is the stun we know. Orderly range the seasons due, and orderly roll the stars. lilow shall we deem the soldier brave who frets of his - wounds and scars? Are we as senseless brutes that we should dash at the well-seen bars?

No, we are here with feet unfixed, but ever as if with lead Drawn from the orbs which shine abave to the orb en which we tread, Down to the dust from which we came and with which we shall mingle, dead.
No, we are here to wait, and work, and strain our banished eyes, Weary and sick of soil and toil, and hungry and fain for skies Far from the reach of wingless men and not tb be:scaled with cries.
No, we are here to bend our necks to the yoke of Tyrant
Time, Welcoming all the gifts he gives us—glories of youth and-prime ; • ' Patiently watching them all depart as our heads grow White as rime.
Why do we mourn the days that go—for the same sun shines each day? Ever a spring her primrose bath, and ever a May her may; Sweet as the rose that died last year is the rose that is born to-day. -

Do we not, too, return: we men, as ever the round earth whirls? Never a head is dimmed with gray, but another is sunned with curls. Bhe was a girl and he was a boy, but yet there are bcys and girls. Ah, but alas for the smile 'pi' smiles that never but one face wore! Ah, for the voice that has flown away like a bird to an unseen shore! Ah, for the face, the flower or flowers, that blossoms on earth no more! • —" The Magazine of Art"--Coemo Moniiionee.

Song of the tea-kettle " Hum-teal dumb-tea!" It is impossible for a man to despair who remembers that his Helper is omnipotent. Be loving, and you will never, want for love; be humble, and you will never want for guiding. A .ehap, being asked to explain the paradox of how it was possible for a lazy man to attain so much educa- tion, answered: "I didn't—attain—it; I--;just heard— it—here—and—there, and was too lazy tolorget it." Weakness works more ill than wickedness; it is easier, between the hand which strikes and the reed which gives way, to defend oneself against the assaults of the former than to guard against the untrustworthi- ness of the latter. Mark Boyd records the ansr,-er the German innkeeper gave to a former Duke of Brus.swick, who; while, travel- ling, had stopped his suite to breakfast at his satberge. When the Duke called for his bill, he obserap-d an enormous charge for eggs, and sent for the landlord, holding the bill in his hand. "Why, eggs must be very scarce in this country ?" "Oh, no your Serene High- ness, eggs are not all scarce, but Orand Dukes are ! Royalty can make puns as well as other beings—our own Royal Family being no exception. The Queen, when Princess Victoria, was one day reading the Roman history: to her noble - preceptress, the 'Duchess of Northumberland. It happened to be the passage where a Roman lady, having visited Cornelia, "the mother of the Gracchi;' after the custom of the time, displayed her casket of precious stones, and called upon the Ro- man matron to produce her jewels in return, when Cornelia brought forward her children, exclaiming with maternal pride, "These are my jewels!" The little Princess here laid down the book, and, looking up into the face of the Duchess, said, "Jewels ! Now I think they must have been Cornelians I" TALICING.—R has been estimated that a public speaker says in one hour, on an average, what, if printed, would occupy fifteen octavo pages. In ordinary conversation words flow from the lips quite as rapidly as in public speech. Supposing, then, that all the talk of one day be estimated as equivalent to four hours' consecutive speaking, a man says in one week what, if printed, would be an octavo volume of 320 pages. In one:year he speaks fifty-two such volumes; and in thirty years he would have an extensive library of 1,560 volumes. It is a matter of rejoicing that the talk of society is not thus printed and perpetuated. Few men, if any, could pass creditably through such a severe test. It is said that Swift, at an evening party, on one occrsion retired to a corner of the room and commenced noting [down the talk of the company. Being-asked what he was doing, he produced the verbatim report of the conversation which had just taken place. Each speaker felt: lament- ably chargnned at the sperficial and trifling character of his utterances. So, doubtless, would every right-minded man feel if some disciple of the phonographic school were always with us plying his pencil whenever we speak. But there is a recording angel by our side. Every word is written, though not by any visible agency. Our conversation exercises a power for good or evil on the mental and moral life of others, and to word as the -vehicle of a thought can pause in its re'ative effect.— Rev. Dr. Hiles Hitehens in The Quiver. Tan HISTORY or PuNervanoN.—Puncturif on is pecu- liar to the modern languages of Europe. It was wholly unknown to the Greeks andßomans ; and the languages of the East, although they have 'certain marks or signs to indicate tones, have no regular system of punctua- tion. The Romans and the Greeks also, it is true, had certain points which, like those of the languages of the East, were confined to the delivery and pronunciation of words; but the pauses were indicated by breaking up the written matter into lines or paragraphs, not by marks resembling. those in the modern system of punc- tuation. Hence, m the responses of the ancient oracles, which were generally written down by the priests and delivered to the inquirers, the ambiguity—doubtless in- tentional—which the want of punctuation caused saved the credit of the oracle, whether the expected event was favourable or unfavourable. As an instance of this kind may be cited that remarkable response which was given on a well-known occasion, when the oracle was consulted with regard to the success of a certain military expedi- tion: "Ibis et redibis nunquam .peribis in bello. ' Writ- ten, as it was, without being pointed, it might be trans- lated either, "Thou shalt go, and shah+ never return, thou shalt perish in battle," or, "Thou shalt'go and shalt return, thou shalt never perish in battle." The correct translation depends on the placing of a-comma after the word nunquam, or after redibis. The invention of the modern system of punctuation has been attributed to the ! Alexandrian grammarian Aristophanes, after whom it was improved by succeeding grammarians; but it was so entirely lost in the time of Charlerhagne.that he found it necessary to have it restored by Warnefried and Alcuin. It consisted at first of only one point, used in three ways, and sometimes of a stroke, formed in several ways. But as no particular rules were followed in the use of these signs, punctuation was exceedingly uncer- tain, until the end of the fifteenth century, when the learned Venetian printers, the Alanutii, increased the number of the signs, and established some fixed rules for their application. ' These were so generally adopted that we may consider the Manutiri as the inventors of the present method of punctuation; and although modern grammarians have introduced some improve- ments, nothing but a few particular rules have been I added since their time..:—Ctuarill's Popular Educator (New I Edition). div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE BIRMINGHAM POULTRY SHOW. The great Birmingham Show was opened on Saturday week, in Bingley Vail, the usual habitat, and closed on Thursday of the psesent week. It has not, we regret to say, been so good as last year, either in respeet to quality or to numbers. The totals are—Poultry 2,339, and pigeons 1,092, or 3,441 in all, as a,gainst 4,1(31 last year. Several things have contibuted to this result, First, as we remarked last week, instead of the usual week intervening between the Crystal Palace and Bir- mingham shows, only one day elapsed from the close of one to the opening of the other, Consequently many birds which would have 4seen at both shows, had the old arrangement been adhered to, could not stand the confinement for so long a period without any interval of rest, and their owners had to choose between one and the other. And in many cases ithe latter show has suf- fered. In addition to this, the very large increase in the number of cattle exhibits—twice as many as last year—necessitated a curtailment of the space given to poultry, and some 300 entries were, we believe, returned. This was, we think, a great mistake, as it seems very strange to invite entries, and then return them without any previous intimation of the fact. Still the number of entries is a large one, but with the growth of other shows this, the oldest existent poultry exhibition, will, soon fall into the background unless some prevision is made (or further accommodation being given to the feathered section of it. In these days of progress, un- less there is advance, there must be a falling la?,ck,— standing still is impossible. A brief summary of the sections is all that we can give here. Of Brahmas there were 337, nearly 50 less than last year. The quality was very good indeed, and many of the specimens wonderful birds. Amongst the county winners we find Mr. J, Manghan, of Liverpool, who wins second for both dark cocks and cockerels; and Messrs. I Birch, of Sefton, second for light cocks, first for dark' hens, and• second for light pullets. Dorkings also showed a falling off in point of numbers, but not in quality. There were 207, or nearly 40 less than last year. Many of the winners were wonderful for size and quality. Mrs. Hind, of Kendal, won third for silver gray pullets; and Mr. R. Smalley, of Lancaster, second for pairs of hens. Cochins were first-rate in quality, though the number exhibited (315) was 59 less than last year. Birmingham is always regarded as the great Cochin I show of the year. Especially in the buff and the par- tridge verities is the quality first class. Mr. J. 0. Rigg, of Ulverston, won first for old buff cocks; Mrs. Barton, of Carnforth, second and fourth for buff cockerels, and second for buff hens; and in the partridge classes Mr. R. Southern, of Worsley, won cup for old hens, and second for pullets. Langshans are growing steadily in favour, but the show at Birmingham has not been as good as might have been expected—certainly far in- ferior to that at the Crystal Palace. Malays are not a very popular breed, but of these there were 72, or, 19 more than last year—one of the few sections that had an increase. Many handsome birds were herein shown, and this breed ought to be better known, as by crossing it produces capital table fowls. The French classes mustered 91 pens, or 17 less than last year. The quality was, however, rather better, and there were very many fine specimens of these valuable breeds. Mr. J. Ainsworth, of Darwen, won second in Creve cocks. The Spanish classes—and in these we in- clude all the sub-varieties—were very, poor in respect to numbers, and not very good in quality, with just a few exceptions. The Black Spanish were very much out of condition. Andalusians were deficient in quality as well as in numbers, and the same may be, said of Leghorns and Minorcas. Plymouth Rocks numbered 40 pens, but they were by no means wonderful in quality. There was a want of size, which we have noticed before. Part of the non-success of this class is due to the scant en- couragement given them at Bingley Hall. Polish showed a decided falling-off, there being scarcely half as many birds in the section as were shown last year. The quality was also much behind, though there were a few good specimens. Mr. P. Unsworth, of Newton-le-Wil- lows, won second for golden-spangled cocks, second for black cocks, and first for black hens; and Mr. A. Hor- rocks, of Leigh, won first for gold-spangled cockerels. The game fowls were undoubtedly the pick of the show, although the entries were about 30 fewer than last year. What has helped to keep up the quality of this section is the competition for two challenge cups, subscribed for by breeders. The one for cocks, value £5O, was won by Captain Heaton, of Worsley, who, as he has won it twice before, now wins it absolutely. He also won 4th for Black Red cocks, 6th for Ceckerels, 2nd and 4th for Black Red Hens; Mr. T. P. Lyon, of Liver- pool, won Ist and 3rd for Black Red cocks; sth for Black Red cockerels, 3rd for Brown Red cockerels, and 3rd for Pile cocks and hen respectively; and Messrs. Ainscough, of Parbold, Wigan, won 4th for Black Red cockerels. Hamburghs were fairly good in'quality, but the numbers greatly reduced in this section also. Game Bantams were 70 less than last year, but the quality was pretty good. Messrs. Ainscough won Ist for old cocks, 2nd for old hens, and Ist for Pile pullets; Mr. T. P. Lyon, Liver- pool, Ist for old hens, and Ist and cure for Black Red pullets; Mr. G. Anderton, of Preston let for Pile Cockerels; Messrs. Stretch, of Ormskirk, 3rd for Pile Cockerels and Pullets respectively; and Mr. W. Shenton, Lancaster, 3rd for Duckwing Cockerel, and 2nd for Pile Pullet. In Bantams, not Game, the Messrs. Birch, of Sefton, won first for Sebrights. Of waterfowl and turkeys there were nearly 70 short of last year, and some of the classes were very badly filled. This was due to the system in vogue of award- ing the prizes to the heaviest birds, regardless of quality —a system which is a bad one, for, though we believe in giving size and weight proper consideration, these

div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—SerranAY.

The House met at 1-15, Lord Monson, owing to the absence from indisposition of the Lord Chancellor, being on the Woolsack. The Earl of Kimberley, Lord Sudeley, the Earl of Cork, Lord Stratheden and Campbell, and the Bishop of Liverpool were the only other members of the House present. ROYAL ASSENT TO THE FRANCHISE BILL. The Earl of Cork, the Earl of Kimberley, and Lord Mon- son retired after prayers, and after a short interval re-ap- peared robed as Lords Commissioners and took their seat on a bench in front of the Throne. The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod having summoned the HORN of Commons, and the Speaker having arrived with the Prime Minister, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Sir C. Dilke, Mr. Shaw Lefevre, Mr. Mundella, the Lord Advocate, and other members, the Royal Commission was read, and 'the Queen's assent given to the follow- , lag measures :—The Representation of the People Bill, the Tramways (Ireland) Act Amendment Bill, the York- shire Registries Act Amendment Bill, the Consolidated Fund Bill. Their lordships afterwards, on the motion of the Earl of Kimberley, adjourned till February 19th. HOUSE OF COMMONS. SATURDAY.

. The Speaker took the chair at 1-25. PAYMENT OF MEMBERS.—Some unopposed returns having been ordered, Mr. H. B. SHERIDAN gave notice that after the Recess he should move in committee of the whole House for leave to bring in a bill to facilitate the return of wolk- ing-class representatives by providiug for the payment of members under certain conditions. Shortly after half-past one, Sir James Drummond, the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, appeared at the Bar, and advancing to the table summoned the House to the House of Peers, to hear the Royal assent given by Commis- sion to several bills agreed upon by both Houses. The S. peaker, followed by about 50 members, proceeded to the Upper House, and on his return, after an absence of 10 minutes, acquainted the LIQUSO that the Representa- tion of the People and other bills had received the Royal assent. The announcement was received with loud cheers. NOTICES.—Mr. AGNEW gave notice that in committee on the Redistribution Bill he should move a clause providing that in the event of a general election all elections in coun- ties and boroughs should be held on the same day.—Mr. McCoax gave notice that after the recess he should call at- tention to commission touting, particularly among the woik- lug classes carried on by insurance agents. A CURIOUS COUNT OUT. .

Lord R. GROSVENOR then moved the adjournment of the House. Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR drew attention to the fact that there were 22 questions on the paper, and expressed the opinion that it was scarcely decent for members to attempt to shirk the duty of answering them. Sir H. WOIXF pointed out that under the new rules to motion for adjournment could be made till all the questions on the paper had been disposed of. The SPEAKER considered that under the exceptional cir- cumstances the noble Lord was justified in making the motion, and being asked by Sir H. Wolff to state what the exceptional circumstances were, the right hon. gen- tleman said there was no government business on the paper. Mr. CALLAN wanted to know whether the House met only for the convenience of the Government? Mr. STAVELEY HILL reminded the Speaker that the ad- journment could not be moved when it was represented that there were matters of urgent public importance to be dis- cussed. The FPEAKER observed that that rule was passed to prevent vexatious and obstructive motions for adjourn- ment. Mr. CALLAN considered the present motion to be vexa- tious and obstructive. Mr. M. GUEST called attention to the fact that there wag not a House, and when, after the usual interval, the Speaker proceeded to count, it was found that there were only 37 members present. Mr. CALLAN called out that the Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs and Aber members of the Government were behind the Speaker's chair. The SPEAKER said the sitting would be suspended till 4-0, and the House would be adjouraed. Lord H. LENNOX : Will the business on the paper be pro- ceeded with then? The SPEAKER: No. Tke right hon. gentleman then retired, and as he did so Mr. Callan raised a cry of "Shame," other Irish members joining in and ejaculating besides "Dirty trick." Mr. Cal-. lan also shouted out " Erriagton, Blennerhassett, Lord Edmund Fitzmaurice, and the Government whips all behind the Speaker's chair." By this time the Speaker bad left tke chair, and the sitting was suspended, but a number of Irish members remained in their places. On the resumption of the sitting at 4,0, the Speaker was greeted by the Home Rule. party with ironical cheers. He at once counted, and finding only 24 members he declared the House adjourned, and left the chair amid rune reed ironi- cal Home Rule cheers. In accordance with the motion agreed to on Friday, the House stands adjourned until Feb. 19.

---E-O-Yl3-T AND THE SOUDAN. REPORTED DROWNING OF 3,000 ARABS IN TILE NILE.

DONGOLA, SuNDAY.—It Is said here that the Mandi, ac- - cepting General Gordon's challenge, tried to make his fol. lowers walk across the Nile, persuading them that the river -would dry up. About 3,000 of his men are said to have been lost in the attempt. Rumours strongly confirm the re- port of the tribal fight with the Mandre troops as telegrahed by me last week, but the native accounts are vague as to the exact locality. Sir H. Stewart, with the Camel Corps, moves from Handek towards Ambukol on Thursday. He will be followed by the Staffordshire Regiment, which con- centrates at Debbeh.—Daily News. DONGOLA, SATURDAY.—A messenger has arrived here from the Mudir's Vakeel at Ambukol. The messenger made the journey from Khartoum in eleven days, and states that the Mandi is cue hour distant from 'that place. Ile adds that General Gordon's General Kashan, Elmoos, with five steamers and 500 men, continued to drive the rebels from the banks of the Nile, and to capture produce as far as Shendy, but waa unable to proceed to Berber owing to the lowness of the river. Lord Wolseley's recent address has produced increased activity among the troops, who are has- tening past this place to Debbeh, the advanced depot. Lord Wolseley and his staff will go to Debbeh shortly. The bag- gage leaves on Monday. Canto. MONDAY—Letters received here from Suakim state that Osman Digma has still great fanatical influence over the tribes, and has collected together between two and three thousand men who are, however, continually slipping away, being tired of fighting. On the first signs of active hostility on the part of the Egyptian or the English Go- vernment, Osman Digma would probably be left nearly alone. He only keeps his men togetLer by extreme severity, killing offenders and deserters f reel uentl y. DONGOLA, TIIESDAY.—The headgearters will be trans- ferred to Ambukol on the 13th instant. All troops are now pushing on there. FIGHTING IN THE SOUDAI,7. _ .

The Daily News sp2cial correspondent at Dongola tele- graphs that further information has reached him respecting the recent attack on Omderman. Two thousand rebels tried to surprise the garrison, and attacked the works with great determination, but were repulsed. Scores of them refused to retreat from the heavy fire, and were killed under the walls of the fort. Despite this signal defeat, °alderman is still besieged. It is said that scarcely any traffic is now carried on with the rebels. They are pressed by famine, and there is greater scarcity of grain daily. Lord Wolseley will leave for Kora on Saturday. EGYPT'S FINANCES. The Russian' Italian, and Turkish Ambassadors had in- terviews with Earl Granville, on Tuesday, in connection with Egyptian finance. CAIRO, TOE'ADdY.—Judgment was given to-day by the Cairo Tribunal of the First Instance in the action by the Caisoe against the Egyptian Government, which was con- demned to refund to tho Caissee the accounts illegally diverted. While the Finance Minister, Mudirs, Receivers, General of Provinces, and M. Le Mesurier and M. Call- lard are personally responsible for the moneys paid to the Government, Nubar Pasha is held not personally respon- sible.

_ CAIRO, TnunsnAs —The Russian and German Diplo- matic Agents successively waited upon the Khedive this morning to demand the appointment of Russian and Ger- man representatives as members of the Caisse of the Public Debt. On their way to the Khedive's Palace they stopped at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and left their identical Notes, in which it is pointed out that Germany and Russia by not having hitherto availed themselves of the right of naming members of the Caisse have not forfeited their right to do so.

div.head: SUEZ CANAL QUESTION.
div.p: THE SUEZ CANAL QUESTION.

..... _ Ismatme, Moxnay.—A canvention has been ratified be- tween the Suez Canal Company and the Egyptian Govern- ment for the construction of a fresh-water canal from Ismailia to Port Said. THE CONGO CONFERENCE. BERLIN, SATLIRDAY.—Sir Edward Malet has declared his intention of drawing the especial attention of the Conference to the question of the slave trade, his Government attaching the greatest interest to the matter. It is believed that the draft of the proposed Convention between England and the African Association reached Berlin to.day.-11-15 P The Committee of the Conference this afte-noon discussed the report of the Sub-Committee upon the Navigation Statutes for the Congo. The report proposes that the navi- gation of the Congo and its tributaries, as also the traffic on side canals and railways to be constructed, shall ha free, and that only duties sufficient to meet the expenses of naviga- tion and traffic shall be imposed. BERLIN, MONDAY, The Conference Committee met to-day at two o'clock. On the question of the free naviga- tion of the Congo and Niger an agreement was arrived at, but the discussion of the neutralisation of the two rivers, with regard to which four projects, proposed respectively by England, Belgium, Germany, and the United Stites, ale before the Committee, and their consideration was not con- cluded.

div.p: FRANCE-THE CHURCLI.-MADAGASCAR.

Penis, MoNDSY.—The Senate adopted all the Clauses of the Senatorial Reform Bit as created by the Committee, and afterwards passid the measure by 130 votes against 24. In the Chamber of Deputies the discussion of the Estimates of

the Ministry of Justice and Public Worship was resumed. M. Lept;re demanded the suppression of the Public Worship Budget. The Chamber declined to accept M. Lepere's pro- posal, and approved Clause 1 of the Budget by 376 votes against 140. Afterwards, however, it adopted the prop's il of the Committee to reduce the salaries of bishops and arch- bishops. A report has been distributed to the members of the Chamber of Deputies containing the depositions of various persons before the Madagascar Credit Committee. Admiral Gralibert stated that the British Government had strenuously endeavoured to bring about an understanding between France and the 11011.9, but bad failed. THE FRENCH MINISTERIAL CRISIS.

PARIS, TIIESDAY.—After a speech from the Premin., the Chamber of Deputies this afternoon recorded its confidence in the Government by rejecting M. Ficquet's amendmentby a majority of 67. ANARCHIST ARRESTS. . .

BERLIN, SIINDAY.-At St. Petersburg OR the night of the 4th inst. twelve Nihilists (ten men and two women), were surprised by the police and arrested in one of the restaurants of the capitll. More than forty arrests were made last week in St. Petersburg. BECHUANALAND.

CAPETOWN, SATURDAY.-----on—t-ie—return journey from Go.ihen, Mr. Upington and Mr. Gordon Sprigg have every- where met with a bad reception, and they have been burnt in effigy at Kimberley and Capetown. THE UNITED STATES.
WAsniNnrox, MON-Dia.—General Grant has written a letter stating that he will not accept a pension, and the bill which had been introduced in the Senate with that object has therefore been withdrawn.

..„ NEW YORK, SLlNDAY.—Farther reductions of wages, dis- charges, and running short time are announced by various industrit s. WASHINGTON, SUNDAY.—The monument erected here to the memory of George Washington has been completed. Ic is 550 feet high. NEW YORII, TUESDAY.—An explosion has occurred at Sharnoken Colliery, Pennsylvania ; seven men were killed. Speaker Carlisle has stated that there will be no tariff legis- lation this winter.

Z ZIBIZS-AT-17-11-;;Y:::111; Hajesty's sloop Osprey Las captured a slave dhow. Upon seeing the English war- vessel the slave dealers threw a nnmbr of the slaves over- board, of whom six were drowned. The slave trade is bask on the coast at the present time. LORD DUFFERIN.

BOMBAY, MONDAY.—The Tasmania, with Lord and Lady Dufferin on board, has arrived. His Excellency and Lady Dufferin are quite well. His Excellency was received by the principal civil and military authorities. Lord Dufferin, in reply to an address presantui to hiss by the Corwation of Bombay, stated that no matter what criticism might be made with regard to his administration, it should not be in the power of any man to say that through fear, favour, or for any personal consideration he had ever turned aside from the course ccndncive to the happiness of the millions confided to his care and to the dignity, honour, and safety of the empire. THE FRANCO CHINESE HOSTILITIES.

PARIS,-T—UES-D tY.-ft is announced this evening that both General Briere de Lisle, commanding the troops in Tonquin, and Admiral Courbet have received instructions to avoid engaging the enemy until further orders, and to remain strictly on the citfensive. Pants, TIIURSDAY.—A discussion on the colonial policy of the Ferry Cabinet took place in the Senate. The Duc de Broglie censured the Government for their policy of expan- sion, and declared it was only suitable for a country which had an overflowing population. Ihe remnbers of the hight, he said, would not vote the Tonquin credit. The Premier, in the course of an,important speech, said that Lord Gran- ville had spontaneously offered his services as mediator, but had not thought it necessary to communicate the Chinese terms to the French Cabinet because they were the same as were rejected in October, 1883. The time for negotiation had passed and the Government, as soon as the credits were voted, would take immediate action. After this de- claration the Senate voted the credits, but the Right took no part in the division. WEST COAST OF AFRICA.

NATIVE —FRIGHrFuL REVELATIONS. CAPE COAST CASTLE, Nov. 17 (VIA LIVERPOOL).—DetaiIs of the riot at Wiunebah, on the 12th just, which has already been noticed by cable, state that it arose from a dispute between two of the town companies. In the fighting which occurred 12 men lost their lives and many were dangerously wounded. It appears there had been rivalry between No. 1 and No. 2 companies for some rime vie, and this was fanned to a flame by a fetish priest from Baracoo, a email town near Winnebah. The fight commenced by throwing stones and finished with the use of cutlasses. Some of the dead found after the fight were liter- ally cut to pieces. As night came on the fight- ing ceased, and about ten o'clnck the district Com- missioner, Captain Birnett, assisted by one of the European residents, entered the town with a small detach- ment of Houssa police and captured over one hundred pri- soners besides seine two or three hundred muskets and all the fetish drums. It is thought that the prompt and deci- sive measures adopted by Captain Barnett -averted a much more dieastrous result and prevented the possible destruc- tion Jf the trading factories. In the fetish IIOUSB was found a kind of pia made in a large brass pan, which upon being examined was found to contain portions of two human bodies. The skulls were smashed in, the victims having been killed by heavy blows. They must have been dead about a week. All is now quiet. The prisoners have been sent to Accra for trial. Many of the wounded have died since the 13th.
SEPARTIT AGITATION IN NORTH QUEENS. LAND.

BRISBANE, WEDNREIDAY=fhO existing depression in Northern Queensland has given rise to a growing separatist movement in the chief northern towns. Public meet:ngs have been held at which the necessity for separation was strongly affirmed, the claim for it being based on the ground that the population of ths north would be double and the revenue quadruple that of Queensland if the separa- tion were effected. TURKEY AND EGYPT.

VIF.NNA, WEDNESDAY.—lntelligence received here from Constantinople states that the last communications made by Musurns Pasha to Lord Granville concerning Egypt for- mulated no proposals. His Excellency has, however, again expressA the Sultan's desire to arrive at a good understand- ing with England on the Egyptian question and to strengthen the ties of friendship between England and Tur- key.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

CONCERT.—A sacred concert was given in the new As- sembly Hall, Kenoble-street, on Monday, in aid of the Con- gregatianal Church Choir Fund. The works rendered were the cantatas " Nativity" and "Jesus of Nazareth." The artistee were :—Miss Richardson, son rano ; Miss Annie Richardson, contralto ; Mr. George Barton, tenor ; and Mr. Tranter, baritone. Dlr. Charles Hewitt was leader of the band. Mr. William Barlow presided at the harmonium, and Mr. F. Barlow conducted. The principals were well received, and Miss Annie Richardson and Mr. Tranter gave every satisfaction. The concert was a success in every way, the hall being well filled. PRESCOT BOARD OF GIIIRDIANS.—The fortnightly meet- ing of this board was held on Thursday, Mr. T. J. Hall pre- siding. A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that in consequence of the death of Mr. Basil Cane they had arranged with Mr. J. J. Henley that he should take charge of those unions in Lancashire which , were included in the late Mr. Cane's district, As Mr. Henley was at present a member of the Boundaries Commis- sion' which duties would probably detain him for two months, Mr. Davy, another Lobel Government Board inspector, would take charge during the interim. A letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the appointment of Mr. Henry Fogg as vaccination officer for the Preacot die- trict,and that his remuneration be 61 in respect of each case of successful vaccination registered by him.—The question of appointing a successor to Mr. D. Swallow, who had resigned the position of assistant overseer for Rainford district, was introduced by the Rev. J. Barnacle. It was de- cided to reduce the poundage remuneration from Is. in the pound to 9d. in the pound. There were four candidates—two local men, named Fairclough and Pennington, who received the highest number of votes ; but as six guardians refused to vote, the clerk ru!ed that no candidate had received a numi,er which could be said to be "a majority of the guardians present." Some confusion ensued, and ulti- mately the appointment was postponed until next board day (Dec. 24). The Workhouse Master reported that there were 449 inmates this week, 453 last week, and 441 in the corresponding period of last year; vagrants relieved last week 31, against 20 in the corresponding period of last year.

The returns of the Volunteer force for 1884, which are now complete, show that the strenLth of the whole fprce exceeds by some thousands the totals of all previous years. There has also been a considerable decrease in the number of non•efficients. . . . .

THE COLERIDGE LIBEL Casn. Mr. Adams, the plain- tiff in the recent cause celebre, has married the Hon. Miss Coleridge. The marriage was quite a private one, not even the bridegroom's own family being invited to the wedding, which took place on the 24th MunDER me IRELAXD.—An exceedingly bad Case of murder was before the Connaught Assizes on Thursday. A msn named Parry, who had been rejected by a young lady named Burns, at Galway, travelled 100 miles to murder her. He committed the crime with a revolver, and afterwards in- flicted a wound on himself. The crime was of a really atrocious and cowardly character, hut the jury recommended the convict to mercy on the ground of the " exasperation" he bad ieceived. lie was sentenced to be hanged on January 13.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his honour Judge Ffoulkes, an important interpleader issue was heard. Toe plaintiff was Joseph Wolff. formerly of Warringtor, the execution creditors were Messrs. Ward and Frith, Sheffield, and the defendant was Christopher Robin- son, of the Eagle file works, Rodney-street, Warrington. Mr. Wellhead, from the office of Mr. Brook, Warrington, ap- peared for tha claiment, and Mr. Ishington (Ishington and Swift, Sheffield) for the execution creditors.—Mr. Wallheed said that the debt and costs had been paid into court. The claimant claimed under a bill of sale dated the Bth March, 1883, and made between Christopher Robinson, Rodney- street, carrying on business as a file manufacturer, and Joseph Wolfe, t'es claimant, who formerly carried on the same business. Mr. Wolfe sold the business to Mr. Robin- son, the defendant in the action, and as security for the price agreed upon, £250, took -a bill of sale on the stock-in- trade.—Evidence as to the bill of sale having been executed was given.—Joseph Wolfe, the claimant, deposed to his transaction with Rohinsm, who was in his employ as fore- man and traveller when the business was made over to him. i The bill of sale eas given as security, and witness had not yet received one penny of the £250. Cross-examined: Witness expected to be paid at the end of six months, but no deflnite arrangement was made as to when the money should be paid. He did not know that the stock of files that were sold to the defendant had been reduced. He knew Rohineon hail no capital when he took the business. He would swear that no conspiracy had been made between himself and Robinson to defraud his (Robinson's) creditors. He was aware that all files that were sold reduced the secerity. Could not swear that the files seized by the execution creditors were the same in respect to which the bill of sale was executed.—Christopher Robinson, the defen- dant, was called, and cross-examined at length by Air. Ishingten as to the extent of his busicess and the number of files sold, with the view of showiog that the files on .yhich the bill of sale was given must have been disposed of in the ordinary course of business, Witness answered some of the questions put to him in a somewhat insolent manner, and was severely censured by his Henour, who said that if witness ditl not take care and answer in a less inso- lent manner he should punish him.—Mr. Ishington said he ' thought that the conduct of the claimant and the defendant, especially of the latter when in the witness box, could not sp:ak in their favour. The way Robinson had evaded qtestione, and endeavoured to avoid giving any statement as what the avenge turnout of files was, seemed to show that there WAS a conspiracy between him and Wolfe, to swear that the files to which the bill of elle referred were the same ones that were seized by the bailiff. He also pointed out that when execution was levied the defendant did not men- tion that there was a bill of sale on any of the articles, and then proceeded to urge several technical objections—After a hearine, occupying about live hours, his Honour reserved his dec;sion.
