Councillor CROSFIELD said that it appeared to him that Councillor Bolton would complain of any statement, even though an angel from heaven made it. (Laughter.) They believed that the scheme was as perfect a one as human being could suggest, but it was impossible to do without the carts going through the • streets. Councillor Bolton wanted something absolutely perfect, which be could not have.

LAO V C• Alderman BURGESS denied that it was proposed to take a sum of money out of capital for the purpose of keeping machinery in repair. In the estimate was included £l2O for each year's repairs, so that it was provided for in revenue. Councillor W. PIERPOINT asked if, in el iscusqinre the pre- _ .

..._ .. , . . posed extension of machinery at Longford, be should be in order in criticising the present machinery as existing .at Longford, and the work that was done there. The CIIAIRIUN: If it bears on the subject now. before
the Council ; but simply to refer back as a matter of history will be out of order. Councillor PIERPOINT said that .it was stated that the . .

machinery hael been and was working well, and in that case it seemed to him strange that they should need any additions at all to it. The report preseuted to the Council in 1879 stated that the collection of 1878-9 was 11,560 tons,

and that after a careful calculation it was estimated that , in a short time the quantity to be dealt with wou'd he 17,600 tons. There was no doubt that in bringing up this particular scheme the committee had taken a pretty wide I margin, and he thought he might fairly assume that as wide 1 a margin WAS taken in the report to which he had referred. ' If the machinery was erected to deal with 17,600 tons it ' seemed rather strange that any extension should be required. With regard to the nuisance, be thought it was as great that day as years past, and as great as it was prior to the machinery being put down. He argued that there was no necessity for the extension, and said that he should oppose the adoption of the report. Councillor Sumer said that daring the last year or two everyone had known that the present machinery at Long- ford had been inadequate to deal with the whole of the re- fuse. It had also been perfectly well understool that the Sanitary Committee were endeavouring to rep ,rt or intro- duce something that they thought would be sufficient to deal with it. The committee after very careful considera- tion, had prepared a report and now came to the Council for support. He thought that those who opposed the report did so as a matter of opinion, with no arguments in support of the course they took. Alderman PlexerEnE said that there was a certain diffi- culty to be overcome, and he thought that if it cost them some thousands a year, it was worth while to do it. By the new scheme there would be a saving, but if not, there would be a serious nuisance overc. me. Councillor BARKER supported the resolution, and Alder- man DAvivs pointed cut that the position now was different to what it was in 1879. The machinery was in fair working condition, and the greater portion of it would last for 20 years. Councillor WHITTLE asked if supposing all was true that was said in favour of the scheme, the present time was not an inopportune one for spending so much money. When they had a 2J. rate for the Ship Canal and a Id. increase on the income tax he said that it was not. On a vote being taken the result was t—For—Aldermen Davies, Holmes, Burgess, Pickmere, and Kean, and Council- lors Dakin, Crosfield, Greening, Barker., Brown, Wright, Roberts, Milner, J. Pierpoint, Francomb, and Sutton. AgainSt—Counoillors Dixon, Taylor, Whittle, Ashton, Hut- chinson,Bolton, W. Pierpoint and Fleming. The meeting then terminated,

Notice of 7i per cent reduction in wages has been given in the Tees district. The premises of Messrs. Guy Brothers, Academy-street, Cork, prnters, lithographers, and stationers, have been de- stroyed by fire. The loss is estimated at 17,000, and over one hundred workpeople have been thrown out of employ- ment. strOCICING DEATH AT OLDHAM.—Shortly after noon on Thursday a shocking affair occurred in a house in Hobson- street, Oldham. Hannah Priestley, aged 58, was found in a , dying condition by a hawker, and she expired shortly afterwards. The deceased was subject to fits, and it is sup- posed she fell against the handle of a washing machine, on which was blood. Her skull was fractured.

ADLIWITON.—The match between these two clubs at Wargrave Moss, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon had a moat unsatisfactory ending, and consider- able illfeeling was manifested by the large crowd of specta- tors who had assembled. The visitors put in an appearance about four o'clock, and owing to their late arrival it was decided to play only 20 minutes each way. The Earles- tonians won the toss and for the first half chose to play with the wind in their favour. Shortly after the kick off the home eleven commenced to press their opponents, and in three minutes Appleton (who was playing as a substi- tute until Ellison appeared), breasted the leather through the goal amid considerable cheers. To the surprise of the home eleven and their supporters the visitors made a claim of " hands" and threatened to leave the field unless their claim was given in. After considerable disputing the Earlestown team consented not to count the goal as a score. No other point was registered up to half-time, though the ' home eleven had had the best of the game. Shortly after the change of ends the visitors made a run up the field, and one of their players sent the leather through the Earlestown goal. POLITICS AND MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. Mr. Chamber. lain, replying to a resolution of the Glasgow Liberal Six Hundred. writes :—" It is an advantage to the Liberal cause in Birmingham to make municipal contests political. A better class of candidates for the Town Council is zot. If politics are excluded the contee't will be fought on personal and petty issues. A Liberal will be more useful in a Town Council than a Tory." WILLIAM EA.DRON IN TROUBLE.—William Hebron, a per. son on whom a good deal of sympathy—and something more substantial—was at one time expended in connection with the Whalley Range tragedy, was sued in the Man. chaster County Court on Thursday by a person on whom he had commiped a brutal assault. Hebron, who is now a beerhouse keel* in Ancoats, was ordered to pay damages to the amount of £25 and costs. TUE LATEST LONDON MYSTIIIIY.—Dr. Thomas ooncluded an icquest in London, on Monday, on the mutilated remains of a woman, portions of whose body were found in various parts of the metropolis. Evidence was also given respecting the discovery of other remains which belonged to another lady. The jury found that the woman bad not died a natural death, and that there bad been either actual or at- tempted malpractices, and it was suggested that the Home Secretary should offer a substantial reward. The latter journeyed to The Pynes, Exeter, on Tuesday. It is understood Mr. H. H. Fowler, M P., has accepted tl 0 post of Under-Secretary of State for the Home Department, iii the room of Mr. ilibbert. The annual meeting of the Central Committee of the Poor Law Conference was held on Wednesday, at Exeter Hall, Lord Enfield presiding. The Queen and Princess Beatrice visited the Dowage7- Duchess of Cambridge at St. James's Palace, on Tuesday. and returned to Windsor in the evening. Two mineral trains came Into collision on the North British Hallway near Airdrie, on Wednesday morning.. Great damage was done, but no lives were lost. A six-ttorey grain store, belonging to the Rothwell-street Storaee Company at Glasgow, was destroyed by fire on Catarday. The damage is estimated at £20.0(50. . .. . ... .. _ _
Mr. Archibald Twee-die, city treasurer of Liverpool, died on Wedneedsy, aged 68 reArs. lie had been connt cted with the Corprraticn since 18.37. aed bad held bis latest office for 28 years.

In sl: the Roman Catholic chapels in Couo,y Wexford (a Dubin correspondent says) collectinns are being made at the rite of 2.1 in the £ on the valuation„for the p iyment of Irish memters of Parliament.

A great demonstration against trawling took place at Aberdeen, on Wednerday, all the ports on the nortL-east coasts being represented. Government interfer.nce in the matter of trawling was called for. The Duke of Richmond presided on Monddy ni,ht at a banquet in honour of Mr. JacJb Wilson. A purse with £3,000 and a piece of plate was prerented te Mr. Wilson in recognition of his services to agriculture. The Chart of Appeal decided on Wedir.sday that Over- seers of the Poor are entitled to their costs incurred in op- poeing a private bill in Parliament which tbrettens toned adnianal burdens upon the rates of their parish. THE LATE CANON GIEDLESTONE —The fLuer.il of the late Canon Girdlestone took place on Tuesday in th.. grave- yard attached to Bristol Cathedral, in the presence of a large gathering of cterry and Nonconformist ministers. The Cambridge University Memo; i ml of Professor Fawcett is to take the form of a portrait, and any surplus funds are 'to be appried to the encouragement of economic science or of some studv conneettd with the welfare of India.

FIRING ON PAPER CHASERS —At 0 liham Pe.:ty Sessions. Hants, on Tuesd.or, JAn Ewers,of Yately Mill, was COM• tnitted fcr trial at Winchester Asssizes on a cbarze of firing at and wounding some students of Wellington College, who were having a paper chase. _ _

A Barnsley hotel-keeper was yesterday Snedps and costs for offending against the Corrupt Practices at Elec bin Act. He had issued a circalar convening a meeting of bur- ge.ses at his house for the purpose of selecting a candidate. There will probably bean appeal against the decision. £lO FOR KILLING A POUTER —in the case of an Eng- lish commercial traveller named Upton Jackson, returned for trial, charged with causing the death of a porter named in Jury's Hotel, the grand jury at Dublin on Mon.! day, found bill for common assiulr, and JaCksen was aistarged on payment of £lO compensation to Kelly's father.

DEAILI OF AN FX-MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT FOR BOLTON. —Mr. Joseph Crook, J.P., who s‘t as member of Parliament for Bolton in the Radical intereat from 1852 to 1862, died on Monday, at hie residence, °Aland., Heaton, Bolt In, aged 75. The deceassd gentleman was a native of the town, and succeeded his father as a cotton spinner in the town, car- rying on business at Spring Miller.

At the Manchester 'Citi Police Court, on Wednesday, Gustave Richaidet, of Prestwich, described as the editor of the Manchester Scholastic Journal, was charged on remand with obtaining £5O by false pretences from Harry Mead, of Chapel-street. Salford. There were other charges of obtain. ing similar sums on various dates from other persons. The prisoner was committed for trial. THE PANIC AT A GLASGOW TFIEITRII—James Turner, the man in custody charged with raising an alarm of Ere at the Star Theatre, Glasgow, and so causing a panic by which 14 persons were killed and as many injured, was liberated by order of the Crown counsel in respect of in- sufficient evidence ts establish a charge of culpable homicide on which he had ten committed for trial. The s atements of witneoses 89 to the locality in the theatre in which the ery of fire was first raised were most con..

DOUBLE EXEC:7I)N AT LIVERPOOL. Arthur Shaw, of Mancester. and Ernest Ewerstadt, a Russian sailor, were executed within the walls of Kirkdale Gaol, Liverpuol, on Monday. Ewerstadt had been condemned to death for the murder of a woman named Himblin,:with whom he had lived at Liverpool. Shaw was hanged for the murder of his wife at Manchester. Shaw confessed his crime ; but the Russian protested his innocence, continuing to do so even when on the scaffold. Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner.

TER OLDEST SERVANT OF THE GREAT WESTERN KIL- LED.—WiLIiam Foruston, aged 8 3 years, a servant in the employ of the Great Western Railway Company at the goods shed at Saltney, near Chsster, %VAS crossing the line on Friday morning just as the nine o'clock express to Pad- dingtm was seen approaching. The poor old fellow was unable to get out of the way in time, and the express struck him en the head, hurled him some distance, and killed him instantaneously. The deceased was the oldest servant of the Great Western Railw,y Company. SMITHFIELD CATTLE Snow—Among the visitors to the Smithfield Chub Cattle Show, Islington. which opened on Monday, were the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Edinburgh, the Princess Louise, and the Marquis of Lorne. There were thirteen entries in the Queen's name, and Her Majesty was awarded two leading prizes in cattle classes. The annual general meeting of the Smithfield Club was held on Tues- day, in the Agricultural Hall, the Earl of Jersey presiding. Satisfaction was expressed at the increased number of ex- hibits and the absence of cattle disease.

DEATH OF A PRESS VETERAN.—The death i 8 reported of Mr. Charles Ross, who might have been described as the father of the Reporters' Gallery in the House of Com- mons. He was long the chief of The Times' staff. He was engaged in the gallery for nearly levy-four years, and was only absent for a brief interval when be managed the Carlisle Patriot. The deceased veteran, when employed on the staff of the Morning Chronicle, reported the pro- ceedings ia Ireland which led to the prosecution of Raniel O'Connell, and was one of the principal witnesses at the trial. Ma. BRADT-8170H AND THE OATIT.—The Judges in the Queen's Bench Division, on Monday, unanimously refused the application of Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., for a rule for a new trial in the case ef the Attorney-General v Bradlaugh, which was tried "at bar," when the jury found against Mr. Bradlaueb in £1,500 as three penalties for having sat and voted in the House of Commons without having first taken the oath as prescribed by law. Execution was stayed for a fortnight to give time for appeal.—On Wednesday, in the Court of Appeal, Mr. Bradlatuth applied for an enlargement of time for appeal, on the ground that he should not be able ta obtain the judges' notes in time. The Master of the Rolls said they would take the case on Monday. THNCONGO Assocetetoe.—A meeting of the Congo Dis- trict Association was held on Wednesday, in Liverpool, to receive the report of three delegates who had attended the Wen African Conference at Berlin in order to advise Her Majesty'a representative upon matters connected with the British trade upen the coast. These gentlemen expressed the opinion that free trade would be established in the terri- tories affected, and that d ifferential d ut les prejudicially affect- ing English merchants would not be permitted. The meet- ing agreed to ask the Government not to delay their formal recnenition of the Belgian International Association, and also to request that men.of-war might be despatched to the African coast to protect the interests of British traders. ACTION AGAINST A CHIEF CONSTABLE.—The County Court Judge at Warwick has given his decision in an action brought by Miss O'Brien' a dressmaker, against Mr. Brab- ner, Chief Constable of Leamington, to recover £5O for damages suotaiaed through the defendant's action. The plaintiff was arrested on a warrant charging her with a common assault, and was detained in a police cell for 43 hours without being taken before I magistrate, although one resided near the station. Mr. Brabner also refused to send for the medical assistance which plaintiff requested, on the ground that she was not able to pay for the doctor's attendance. His Heuour said that in law it was the defen- dafet's duty to bring the plaintiff before a justice without unreasonable delay, and he should also have allowed Miss O'Brien to communicate with a medical man. He gave judgment for the plaintiff for £5O. Notice of appeal was given. THE ASTON RIOTS.: END OF TULE CASE.—The bearing of the charges in connection with the Aston disturbances was resumed at Birmingham on Saturday. The summons iesued by the Liberal Association against Mr. Jarvis, charg- ing him with misdemeanour, by making a false declaration. was about to e taken; but immediately on the opening of the court the Stipendiary made an annonucement which settled the whole of the esses.—Mr.Kynrersley said : Since the adjournment on Friday I have considered this matter. No doubt the case is of great importance, and it has, no doubt, keen greatly exaggerated ; but I think tbe public won't be satisfied unless the case goes before a jury. I think, therefore, the better plan will be to send it to a jury in this manner. I shall refuse to commit in this case, and leave you to your remedy under the Vexatious Indictment Act. If you wish to go on, of course, you may.—Mr. Young (after a pause): I understand the case against Reed is dis- missed. That being so, I may take upon myself the respon- sibility of a step on behalf of the Liberal Association. Of course, I have not been engaged in this case for a number of days without having considered every possible aspect of it which it was likely to assume; and I shall take upon my- self the responsibility of assisting you by the course which I am now about to take in trying to put a stop to these pro- ceedings, which I quite agree are, for the most part, scanda- lous. Ido not propose to offer any evidence on the counter charges—The whole matter is therefore apparently disposed of. _ _

div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1884.

THE Conservatives of Warrington have not yet quite emerged from the fog in which they were enveloped for so long while everybody else was enjoying the bright summer weather. , Notwithstanding that ward meetings were j held in the elrly part of the year at which such of the Conservatives as were present pledged themselves to do their best to return Sir GILBERT GREENALL at the next' election, 1 it was obvious that things were not in apple- pie order—that with regard to the Brewer of Wilderspool pleslging himself to " stand " as the Tory candidate, it was still a question of "to be or not to be." Then came the ominous rumours of another candidate being brought forward—followed by the explosion of laughter at the discovery that Kr DANT4r. , ADAMBoN had been Suggested in happy ignorance of his being a Liberal, and, lastly, the out-and-out declaration on the Dart of Sir GILBERT himself, at the opening of the , Conservative Club, that he had at last decided to accept the invitation which had been given . him to contest the constituency. This Vaght to have settled matters, ar.,‘,l it did for a tline-5. Very short time, P.n.' when the " rear- , ing dinner ' came f.'s', be given—it was very ; much in arrn-r, by-the-bye, seeing that tt followed l'he formal opening—the avtrage Sonstl.vative was bewildered by th rinounce- , Ittnt of a candidate for Parliamentary honours in the person of Mr. ROBERT PIER- I POINT. To Liberal on•lookers, with the weather eye open, it was pretty plain that , the reference to, Mr. PIER POINT was made by way of securing what the lawyers call a re- versionary interest. But Tories in a fog ' knock themselves against the most. extraor- dinary things, and the result has been, to ' speak phrenologically, the addition of a few , " bumps " before they could get the bearings of the situation. And when they are got they are certainly curious; for under the present arrangement, an arrangement con- ' secrated on Monday night by the blessing of: Captain REYNOLDS, they have got two candi- dates on their hands—one for the "next election" and the other for "the next after that." It is a case, so far as the candidates are concerned, of—to quote a Mayoral quo- tation—" the old Obediah and the young Obediah ; " while the mystified constituents j are left to sing— How happy could I be with either Were t' other dear charmer away.

•And how awkward it would be if the electors should continue— But, whilst they both tease me together, To neither a word will I say They were both together on Monday night, and th-y were both engaged in the teasing process, "the young Obediah " acting for the time being as chairman for "the old Obediah." This is all very good, of course, so long as it lasts ; it is pleasant to see brethren dwelling together in unity, if for a few hours only ; though, to be candid, we have not much hope of matters being really mended by this public exhibition of the game of "waiting for dead men's shoes "—more particularly as the shoes" in question are in possession of a hostile " party " that shows no disposition to surrender them.

Milling to Sir GILBERT GREENALL'S speech, for as yet he occupies the first place in the "forlorn hope" which the Tories are fighting in Warrington, we find a somewhat doleful reference to the fact that his followers are few in his remarks upon the " small attendance" at the ward *meetinT,on•Monday, at the Con- servative Club. It would seem, therefore, that the premises in Sankey-street which were erected to "house all the Conservatives of the town" have already been found needlessly large, seeing that with one candidate in .the chair and another on his feet it is impossible to more than half fill one room. Can it be that even Conservative working-men are getting tired of the rAveet nothings" of Sir GILBERT GR RENALL ? They may tolerate once in a while a speech which is all begin- ning, and that beginning saturated with ful- some compliment of each preceding speaker; but when, time after time, there is " only this and nothing more" we think they may be excused if they finally resolve to stay at home. It may be that some of them like Sir GILBERT'S ale better than his

THE Financial Reform Association has for over twenty years, in season and out of season, done a wonderful work in the way of politically educating the people of this coun- try. It may be that its publications have not been commonly found in the hands of the British workman' but he has nevertheless had the benefit of them. Statistics are not as a rule very cheerful reading, but they often form the backbone of an argument; and, rightly used, they sometimes carry a convic- tion with them which becomes of permanent influence. It is thus that the piles of figures of the invaluable Almanack issued by the Association have come to be factors of great mament. If they are not studied so directly by working-men as we think they ought to be, they are brought to them in various ways by writers and speakers who make good use of the publications of the Association. The Almanack for 1885 is just out, and we com- mend it to ;he attention of our readers. It is such a veritable mine of political information that the shilling sunk in it is soon found to become a spir.d!d in- vestment. The circulation, large though it is, does not by any means cover the cost of producing the work. On that account re- former,s would do well to try to stimulate the sale, and thus help to send it rejoicing on its way. The members of the Association, with Mr. E. K. MUSPRATT, J.P., as President, are not, we are aware, to a trifle in the way of expenditure when they are sowing good seed, and they are admirably served by Mr. HAMPDEN JACKSON as editor, and Mr. ALFRED CRILLY as secretary. Now and again we find one or another set of figures questioned by " prentice hands," with the result that the Almanack has another feather added to its cap. Indeed, so well established is its reputation for accuracy that Tory and Radical alike turn to its pages when forging armour with a view to battle. The new issue is a distinct improvement in some respects upon any of predecessors. The index has been consi- derably enlarged, so that there is now na difficulty in getting quickly at any sper:. item of information. The' House of • "a d and dealt with under various 11-ads, now full list of the reor ° there is f[ms which have been thrown out by that mischievous arm of the State. A 'foie is given of the "extent of benefit 'rived from public revenues by the aristOcracy," and it is found that the total is hot less than Lroaooo,ooo—a sum so vast as almost to take away one's breath in_naming it. New features have been added giving statistics in relation to War, Education, Local Taxation, Agriculture, &c ; and altogether it must be said of the Almanack that it is as full of information as an egg is full of meat.

ThBSnAMERS BETWEEN WIDNES AND LONDON.— The BB.Shap Fell, of the Fell line of steamers, left West Bauli'Aock on Friday with a general cargo of wire glass, I P:austic, bicarb mate of soda, and coals of considerably more than 450 tons, for London. The steamer will run regularly between Widnes and London, West Bank Dock having been selected as the shipping place for the goods of the principal firms of Widnes, Bt. Helons, and Warrington. The action has been taken in consequence of the inability of the manu- facturers of the district to obtain any reduction of the rail- way rates, and the new venture, in which many of the leading firms have cs-operated, is expected to prove very successful, and of the utro...st benefit to the extensive trade of Widnes.

Pusuc opinion seems to be ripening on the question of Lotteries at Bazaars. It is felt that it is gross partiality to fine a trade- man or publican £ o for selling racing lottery tickets, as has been the case at St. Helens, whilst immediately afterwards the law is flagrantly broken at a Bazaar in the same town, and no notice is taken of it by the authorities. We do not suggest that "a: policeman in disguise," as the phrase is, should be sent to Bazaars with a view to pouncing on the first clergyman he finds "keeping open a lottery ;" but we do urge j that some action should be taken by the au- thorities with a view to putting a stop to ' practices which are a scandal to religion and I a discredit to the community. Perhaps the best way of proceeding would be to follow the course taken by the Watch Committee of Birmingham who have caused it to be made known that Birmingham, the future they will prosecute persons known to have taken part in raffles or lotteries at Bazaars. Mr. WHITE, clerk to the borough magistrates of Warrington, points out, in a letter which will be found in another column, that a prosecution can be jinstituted by any person whatever against , those who are thus guilty of a breach of the law, and the title to take proceedings holds ' good " for six months after the commission of the offence." This being the case, it will Ibe seen that ministers, deacons, church- wardens, and stallholders undergo not a little I risk when they seek to estalish a brisk busi- ness in lotteries. They had better mind what they are about, or they at any rate may find the "lucky bag" the reverse of lucky. It can be nothing to- be proud of to escape with even a nominal fine, when there is the knowledge that they have rendered themselves liable to imprisonment for three months with hard labour as "rogues and vagabonds." We understand that at Christ Church bazaar, Latchford, as well as at St. Mark's, St. Helens, several magistrates took part in the raffling; and we cannot but think that they were setting a bad example, not to mention the risk they ran, and are still running. It is time that this sort of thing came to an end; for it cannot be much longer continued with- out somebody putting in motion the ma- chinery of the law. It would savour of malice for a private individual to take action; pro- ceedings, when they are taken, should be taken by a public officer, and under the direc- tion of the local authorities.

RUNCORN Butztat, BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday, Mr. James Handley in the chair. Present: Messrs. Coleburn, Moss, Rogerson, Littler, Briecoe, and Salkeld (secretary). The Secretary reported that for the eight months ending November 25th there had been 239 interments, against 292 in the corresponding period last year. The fees received during the same period amounted to £264 .143 Id, being an increase of £47 83 lid in the corresponding period last year. Accounts amounting to £35 Be 101 were pas-ed for payment. The Secretary also reported that he had received from the overseers the earn of £1.20, and had invested in Consols £125 Ss 21. Cheeraes were signed for interest falling due amounting to £3l 17s 51. Subsequently an enter- tainment was given in the chapel, under the presidency of Mr. 'I. Edwards, of Liverpool. The choir from Milton-road Congregational chapel rendered several anthems in good style, and glees were well sung by two quartette parties, the first comprising Miss Thomas, Miss Coverley, Messrs. J. Miss Travis ably officiated an accompanist. The proceeds of the 1 ' entertainment will ba devoted to the chapel fund. SALE OF WORK AT WIDNES.—With th 5 Object of liquidating the debt upon the boundary wall of St. Ambrose Church, Widnes, a sale of work was held in Page-lane Schoolroom, on Thursday. The wall was ended at a cost of £550. Towards this sum £l6O had been raised by a bazaar and a sale of work. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis had sub- scribed £25, Mr. F. H. Gossage £25, Messrs. Sullivan and Co. £1.6, Mr. G. Pilkington £3O, and other amounts, leaving a balance of £l9. The present sale of work, which was ex- pected to wipe off this small balance, had been arranged by the children of Ihe Sunday School, who had undertaken the labour and responsibility under the guidance of Mrs. Riley. There were three stills—the work stall, the toy stall, and the refreshment mall—all well laden with goods; and tended by the children themselves. The Rev. S. A. Spooner opened the proceedings in an appropriate speech. During the evening Mr. Davies delivered phrenological lectures and examined heads, and a good sum was realised in this way. Row IN THE NELSON INN, RUNCORN.— At Runcorn Petty Session on Monday, Patrick Wlfelan, a young man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Nelson Inn, High-street, and with refusing to quit when requested • by Thomas Shepherd, the agent for the landlord.—Shep- herd stated that on the night of the fourth inst. the defen- dant rushed into the house like a mariman, and created a great disturbance. He attacked witness and several other p rsous in the bar with great violence, and it was with diffi- culty he was ejected.—The defendant said be and his father before him had spent as much money in the " Nelson "as " here and there one," and he did not think he would have been summoned for what he had done—The defendant was fined 20s and costs, or 14 days' hard labour. A DISHONEST PEDLAR AT RUNCORN. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, James Parker, a pedlar, was char- ged with stealing half a sovereign belonging to George Sef- ton, labourer, of 5(3, Surrey-street. About noon on Saturday Me Sefton purchased front the prisoner a packet of needles, for which he asked a penny. She gave him what she , thought was a sixpence, and received 51 ch tnee, but he had I not proceeded far when she discovered Viet she had given him half a sovereign. She followed him and acq tainted hiMof this fact, but he with a peat show produced his purse and denied that he had received a half sovereign from her or had one about hint. THE PRESCOT GUARDIANS AND THE ODDFELLOWS.—The recent action of the Presoot Board of Guardians in declining to grant relief to a person named Southward, on the ground that he was not a pauper, because he received a certain sum from the funds of an Oacifellows' lodge, of which he had beena member, appears to have created a strong feeling among Oddtellows of the district, as well as considerable in. terest in other parts of the country. "The Oddfellows' Magazine" for December contains a leader on the subject, headed" Boards of Guardians v. Pauper and Pauper Luna- tic Friendly Society Members." The article states :—" In common with our members generally we bad hoped that after the success attendant on our efforts in 1877-8, we had heard the last of Poor Law officialism asserting itself against the rights and privileges of members of friendly societies. But notate Local Bumbledon is found from time to time . asserting itself, is seen dragging society officers before magistrates and county court hedges, and is too frequently found at work striving to secure its pound of flesh, strain- ing the law to its utmost, even in direct antegoninn to all principles ef common sense, philanthropy, and equity. But in saying this, it must not be thought we are reproba- ting tire general policy of boards of guardians generally in such matters. We are aware that in the majority of in. stances, when the case of a friendly society member is broureht before a well-constituted hoard, especially in town districts, and especially where there is to be found a lib rale minded chairman, a most liberal interpretation is given, and the law is even strained in favour of the provident society member in preference to the unthinking and 'improvident non-member. But there are exceptions to this procedure, and one ruch exception is made notably manifest i . in the letter appearing n our last from Brother / Fidler, the esteemed C. 5, of the St. Helens / (Laacashire) dietrict of our society. LOW LIFE IN WIDNES : DRINK AGAIN.

Yesterday Mr. W. T. Huslsand, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the White Star Hotel, Widnes, on the body of _Catherine Johnstone, aged 33 years, who died at a house in Dock-street on Wednesday morning.—Evide.nce was given by Louisa Monaghan, wife of Thomas Monaghan, labourer, of 29, Dock-street ; Ann Dooley, wife of Jamts Dooley, labourer, 21, Dock-street ; and James McKinley, labourer at the Atlas Chemical Works.—lt appeared that the deceased, who was a widow, was a native of Chester, and four years ago met McKinley at Wrexham. They had since lived together as man and wife, although they were not married, and had been known to the witnesses for the past twelve months as a couple who were much addicted to taking intoxicating liquors. About a week ago the de- ceasrd and McKinley went to live with Monaghan. The deceastd hod just passed through a severe drinking bout, and a;t'aough there was plenty of food in the house she was unable to partake of it, but would "drink anything she could get.' On Tuesday night she complained of a pain in her stomach, and on Wednesday morning about six o'clock, just previous to McKinley going to work, she asked him for a penny in order that, with the halfpenny which she already posseFsed, she might purchase a gill of beer. McKinley had not a coin in his possession, and ad- vised her to borrow Id. from a neighbour. Later, deceased complained to Mrs. Monaghan of Vac pain she was suffer- ing, and the latter endeavoured about half-past eight to obtain a penny from Mrs. Donley, but without saccess. On returning she found the deceased ;ying across the hearthstone, and Mrs. Dooley and other neighbours were calei in. Mrs. Dooley at once ran for the doctor, but when ehe returned in about five minutes afterwards life was extinct. The deceased had a sister in respectable cir- cenwances at Chester.—Several jurymen said they had seen the woman getting drink, but had never seen her far gone in drink.—Mr. Miller (the foreman) point,d out that there was plenty to eat, but the woman could not eat it.— Another Juryman: There 489 plenty of furniture in the , room to eat the food off, (Renewed laughter.)

A jury man had previously Informed the reporters that there WAS not a scrap of proper furniture in the lower rooms of the house, and that the body of the deceastd was laid actors two soap boxer, and covered with a single sheet, while a bacon box served the occapalts ot ths house as a table. The coroner said if the jury were not perfcctly satisfied that the woman died through drickltig it PM a pity to r cord such a verdict —Mr. Miller Shers is nothing tor Ant to foul play.—The Coroner: That is the greet °Viet of ' the inquiry.—Another juryman thought that the deceased died through neglecting to sustala herself wittr proper food. He bad seen her, about four or five days, in 4 weak what people called "three sheets in the winci;t After SOIII3 conversation, a verdict 'was returned to the effect that the deceased probably 'Med from neglect and I want of proper nourishment, but thvt as to the exact cause of death there was not sufficient evi.lence to show,

OUR LONDOINT LETTER-.

LONDON, THURSDAY. It is many years since a Parliamentary recess was re much enjoyed by members as the current one. It is Cherished not only fer what it is, but from consideration for what it might have been. Had the Lords persisted in their mad determination to throw euragain the Franchise Bill the closieg of the Parliamentary session would have been the signal for a renewal of the fight in the provinces, with the prospect of a noisy session immediately 1 ollowing. As it is we have stetmed out of rough water into a pond, and members have given themselves up with acute satisfac- tion to home delights or the opportunity for foreign travel. It is, perhaps, a little bard for the daily newspapers which have hitherto bad a suofeit of topics forsdiscussion and which now helplessly wander around, thankful for a cattle show and deeply grateful for a storm in Vienna. In these circumstances General Gordon and Lord Wolae- ; ley's expedition will be partially reinstated in the promi- nent position formerly held by them. General Gordon however, can never expect to be the object of such ittense interest as he was during the early spring. From the time of his departure noisily expressed interest in him has been concurrent with the drift of political events at home. If by any accident the Ministry seemed shaken and no news had been heard from Gordon for a few days or weeke, there arose a mighty gust of passionate desire for his earety, and indignant denunciation of a Government who in order to rescue Gordon at the time the cry first arose should have degpatelied to relief expAition tive or six weeks before Goidon himself started it is now clear that this gallant soldier is not only in a stre of perfect safety, but is now, as he has frequently been during the past ten months, in a position to leave Khartoum. Besides, the cry even in its most prosperous times never did as well as might have been expected. The English people are not slow to recognise conspicuous gallantry and consammate military skill. But they have always felt that General Gor- don started upon his mission with views directly opposed to those of the Government, and that A hen he found him- self in opposition to his instructions he took his own way. It is much pleasanter to express admiration for the brave soldier than it is to discuss the wilful and inconsiderate man. Consequently we have heard the most generous praise bestowed upon Gordon. At the same time a sense of. the true position of affairs has been present in the minds of a clear-sighted people. Thus the cry raised for party pur- poses though shrill and prolonged has always failed of the desired effect, and seems now permanently hushei. There Seems now little doubt of the safety of Vitzittele, who went out to the Soudan as correspondent for the Morning Advertiser, and was supposed to have perished with the army of General dicks. There hare from time to time been rumours of a white man in the camp of the camp of the Mandi, who has generally been described as acting as a doctor. Lord Wolsoley has now convinced him- self (hit this is the missing journalist, and is c-tfieent that he will be able to rescue him. Should Vitzittele come home what a bocZte will be able to make! He has hem more or less attached to journalism for many years without securing a place in the front rank. But his uniqns opportunitiea will surely inspire him to the making of a valuable and in- teresting book, which will be .nuch sought for by London publishers.

Talking about newspapers, New Year's Eve will witnasS the death of a paper that has made a long and desperate struggle with adverse fortune. This is the Edinburgh Daily Review, started many, years ago in opposition to the Scotsman, and as an organ of the Free Charon. Money has been lavished like water upon the enterprise. But the Review never had a chance from the day of its birth. Scotchmen have a regard for the Scotsman, which far ex- ceeds that which in its palmiest days the Times extorted front the English public. It rrquired an uncommonly goad newspaper to undermine the influence of the older journl4 and the Review never was a good newspaper.

I mentioned last year a little comedy that had been got • up for the amusement of the Prince of Wales. It took place at the house of a well-kwavn lady, who is frequently hon- ored with a visit from the Prince and his little personal court. On that occasion the hostess, whom we will call Mrs. 8., was informed that the French Minister, M. Wad- dington, was in Cowes, the scene of the little comedy. The Prince of Wiles expresrd a desire to meet his Excellency at dinner, and an invitation was at once forwarded, and , promptly accepted. After dinner M. Waddington, who ap- I paarcd to have dined sufficiently, began to discuss with Lord Charles Beresford-the ormrpsrative merits of the English and French' Navies. 'From words the two combat- ants got to blows, and Mrs. 13., to her profound dismay, be- held the representative of the French Republic set upon in her drawing-room in the presence of the Prince of Wales. Lord Charles literally beetled M. Waddington out of the room. The fight was renewed in the garden, and finally the unfortunato. French Minister was bundled over the gar- den wall, whence be presently returned with his coat torn. Mrs. B. set herself with anxious zest to bring about a truce, and the Prince of Wales, controlling as well as possible his boisterous laughter' joining in the good work, the French Minister and Lord Charles Beresford shook hands, and to all outward appearances became good friends. This was too good a story to be kept private. It travelled far enough to reach the French Embassy at London. M. Waddington made a formal communication to Earl Granville, with tie result that explanations were forthcoming, showing that "Billy "Russell, who in early days won fame as a special correzpondEnt of the Times bad, for the amusement of hin Prince, personated M. Waddington, and had suffered himself to be hustled over a garden wall.

The success of this moot huniourons and ptincely enteran: ttinment led to a desire to emulate it. But tb:.„ .a Year though the humour Of the eemedy IS Ver,7, filiadi 'akin to that of last year, the play Is hot quite So drathatic or so per- fect in its characterisation. After this year's dinner at the urns house, the guests being once more in the drawing- room, there entered an old woman in French costume with skirts perhaps a little shorter than are usually seen either in town or province. After being taunted a good deal the old lady was asked if she could dance. She replied that if some one would play she would see what she could de. Some one stock up a tune once well known at the Mehlle, and I played even now at the Jardin de Liles, and the old lady with extraordinary vigour danced the cancan. After this the mysterious visitor claimed the hand of the Prince of Wales in a quadrille, and thereafter disappeared as myste- riously as she had arrived. The old lady was subsequently ' identified as a hoary•headed English Admiral, who did not think it below his personal dignity or his official position thus to amuse his Prince. The entertainment was not lack- ing in vivacity or success, but it was agreed that it should have come before rather than have followed after the in- imitable performance which came to a climax when "Billy" Russell, puffing, snorting, and swearing, was bundled over the garden wall by "Charlie" Beresford. I wonder how many people know that the sacks which bring over flour from America are made of paper? I con- fess I dii not till the ethe.r day, when by chance instructed. Not only are the flour sacks now in daily use made of paper, but they have been so for nearly 20 years. The necessity arose at the time of the civil war in America, when cotton was driven up to a price that made it prohibitive as a material for manufacturing sacks. Necasity here, as else where, was the mother of invention. The paper in-ordinary use in Japan is one of the tough- est I know. It is so strong that shopkeepers habitually use it instead of string. I have now come strips of paper which tied up a parcel I bought in Tokio, and which I have since had in use for tying and retying papers. The curious thing about the Japanese is that they have not yet succeeded making good writing paper. There are po.sibilities of A unique note paper in their raw material. What they pro- duce doeaawell enough for them, since their pert is a brush. They could, if they gave their minds to it, turn out a beau- tiful product which would take by storm London society, which is always running mad after eotnethiug new in note- paper.

DRUNXENNESS.—The following cases were dealt with : Luke Tully, fined 103 and costs ; Thomas Boyle, Joseph Dagnall, and James Boardman, 5s and costa each ; Martin Higgins, 55 including costs. TnErrs.—James Miles, a Militiaman stationed at Orford Barracks, was sentenced to a month's imprisonment for stealing nibs of beef, valne is al, from the shop of John Cross, butcher, Golden-squar e. —Mary Ireland, an old woman, was fined 10a and costs for stealing a quantity of coal, value 31, the property of Charles John Holmes, on the 3rd inst. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS : STABBING " A DONKEY.— Edward Brown was summoned for ill-treating a donkey on the 29th ult. He r,-as seen on that day—Warrington horse fair—driving a donkey in Dial-street. With a short stick pointed at one end he " stabbed " the animal violently on the off-side of the back, causing it to jump about and kick. —lnspector Nicholls, who proved the case, said it was a common practice to goad asses in that manner. Defendant was fined lOs and costs.—Thomas Armstrong was summoned for working a horse in an unfit state on the 4th inst., rnd John Lunt, the owner of the horse, for allowing it to be so worked. The former was fined ss, and the latter 103 with the costs. SNOWBALLING THE SALVATION ARMY.—James Walsh and George Hopkins, young men, were summoned for throwing snowballs on Sunday, November 30th, to the danger of passengers, in Horsemarket-street. They were seen by P.C. Corcoran pelting the members of a Salvation Army procession. The Bench fined them 53 and costs each. —Alfred Barker, a boy, charg,Qd with throwing snowballs in Lythgoes-lane, was let off with a caution. MIK.ELLINEOVS.—James Warburton and Thos. Howard were summoned for allowing nuisances to exist on their property, the former at Kinder's-yard, Latchford, and the latter at Knutsford- road. WARRINGTON BoA.IID OF GUARDIANS. Th 3 fortnighily meeting of this Board was bold at the , Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present— Messrs. Cooper (in the chair), Derbyshire, Jolley Black- hurst, Brown, Hunt, William Houghton, Hun;phreys, Greenell, Appleton, John Houghton, Jeans, Grange, Fors- ter, Harrison, Rev. F. G. Roberts, and S. button (assistant clerk). CIIIIISTMAS HISSERS : BEER FOR THE INMEOES. The House Committee recommended that the usual Christmas dinners be provided for the inmates of the Work- house and officers, with beer.—Mr. BROWN moved the adop- tion of this minute, and Mr. APPLETON seconded.—Mr. DARBYSILIRE said he begged to move an amendment th the minutes be passed whh the exception of that giving the inmates beer. He ,phjected to givieg them bee: on principle He objected because it was unnecessary and an expense which was not juetifiable, and which they ought not to acir the ratepayers to pay. He did net think it was a proper way of commemorating Christmas Day, and as far as his judgment went, and from what he lame heard, Chrietmas Day would be much better got through without beer than with beer. The inmates did without beer during the year except for medicinal pur- poses, and he did not see any reesen whatever why they could not do without it on Christmas Day. They would do much better bodily, and sp4itually they would be much better without beer. Therefore he moved his amend- ment. —Mr. BUNT seconded this amendment, and said he quite endorsed all that Mr. Derbyshire had said, although he (Mr. Hunt) had no particular objection to beer.—Mr. JOLLEY supported the propesal of the committee, and sal 1 that as one of the Hones Committee he should do as he did last year, and snpport tha proposal that the inmates have each a glass of "nut brown ale' to warm their hearts and make them have cheerful ccuntenances. Not only that, he should like, with the permission of the House Committee, to give the inmates a little food for the mind by sending to them a number of Graphics and ether illustrated papers (Hear, hear.)—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE said that would do them more good than beer.—Mr. JOLLEY thought that Mr. Derby- shire would give him credit for being charitable—(hear, hear)—and as long as he had the privilege he would vote for the inmates having this glass of beer on Christmas Day. —The CILIIRUAN also supported the proposal of the com- mittee, which on being pat to the meeting was carried, only the mover and seconder of the amendment voting against it.—The Schools Committee also r commended that the scholars and officers at Padgate Industrial Schools have the usual Christtnas dinner, the ofEcers being allowed to sub- stitute turkey and geese for road beef.—This recommendee tien was adopted.

. -- A letter was read from the Local Government Board refer- ring to an enclosed communication which they had received from Mr. M. Birkla.ad, of Earlestown, respecting the recent appointment by the Guaraians el an assistant clerk. In this connection Mr. Birkhead called the attention of the Local Government Board to what he considered to be the irregular election of the assistant clerk. If he rightly understood the Consolidated Orders due notice of every such appointment ought to be given and candidates invited by advertising, so as to prevent offices at the disposal of the Guardians becoming matter for special family arrangement In conclusion the Local Government Bard invited the observations of the Guardians with respect to Mr. Birkbead's letter.—The CHAIRMAN said that the clerk (who was away on the busi- ness of the Board) sent word that he should like the discus- Mon on the subject postponed till he returned.—The Assis- ts:cr. CLERK said he ought to mention that that morning the assent of the Local Government Board to the appoint- ment of assistant clerk bad been recsived. Ile al.so added that the appointment hod not been made irregularly.—Mr. HARRISON said he ventured to say that the appointment was most irregular. He knew such a course had never been adopted before, He then referred to the Orders bearing on the subject.—Mr. APPLETON' also contended th it the ap- pointment had been made irregularly, and, referring to [h.; appointment of the committee which dealt with the in- creases of salary, said Mr. Derbyshire, the chairman of the committee, had, so far as he (Mr. Appleton) was aware, I refused to be appointed to the committee at the Board meet- ing, but seemed to have been put on afterwards —Mr. BLACKHURST thought it was not worth their while discussing that subject. The Local Government Board bad sanctioned ! the appointment of assistant clerk, and they would not alter their decision.—Mr. DARBPSHIRE also agreed that the matter had been settled by the Local Government Board, arid the thing was really done with. He should, however, just like to say with regard to Mr. Appleton's statement about him (Mr. Darhyshire) that it bristled with untruths. He was not surprised at the statement knowing from whom it came —(laughter)—but still he wished to say th tt it was incor- rect as far as be was concerned.—Mr. HARRISON thought that for one member of the Board to brand the statements of anotker as untruths was most indiscreet and uncalled for. Mr. Appleton's reputation at that Board was, ha thought, such as to justify them in bolding a very opposite opinion. —After a little further discussion, Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved a motion that the Board proceed to the neat business,which was carried.

A letter was read-fr-oni-1;11;:-B-rietiey, clerk to the Newton Commissioners, asking the Board to pay an account amounting to £3O Os 4d in respect of a man named Harris, who bad been in the Warrington Infirmary, stating that un- less the account was paid further proceedings would be taken,-Mr. AreLrroti said the difficulty in this case seemed to arise SS to whether the family were paupers or not. Dr. Watkins had ordered him to go into the Infi.mary on be- half of the local authority.—Mr. JEANS: Then let the local authority pay for him.—The ASSISTANT CLERK said the patient seemed to have been taken to the Infirmary without an order previously having been obtained from the relieving officer, and the question was whether the Guardians could pay the account even if they would.—Mr. LionT said Dr. Watkins, who was medical officer both for the Guardians and the Newton Commissioners, took upon himself to re- move the patient to the hospital. The man was certainly not a pauper either when he went into the hospital or when he came out —Mr. DARBYSHIRE proposed that the con- , sideralan of the account be postponed till their nest meet- ing, and that the relieving officer in the meantime report the whole facts of the case to the clerk.—Mr. HENT So. cor.cl3:l this proposal and added that he hoped the matter wor.'.e be settled amicably.—The proposal was carried.

SHOOTING A FOWL AT BILLINOE.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, James Latham, Billings, was summoned for unlawfully shooting a cock belonging to Mice Roble—lt seemed that defendant was empleyed by a farmer on whose land fowls frequently trespassed. Com- plainant said sha saw him fire a gun at and kill a valuable cock belonging to her which was in one of his master's fields—Defendant said he was told to shoot all fowls that he found on the land, and all the people living about there had been warned to keep their poultry out of the Set:le.—Mr. Eckersley said he had no rigkt to ehoet the fowl, although It was trespassing. He would Le fined se, the value of the fowl.—Mr. Haskell said the complainant also ought not to allow her fowls to go on the land. FOOTBALL.—HayIock Temperance Ist v. Oaddam, Adam Hong, A. eldeillop. and other genVemen.—The CHAlReLes,e4id that when it was originally decided to bold two or threeemeetingea in that part of heid6ChEshire it wee thought their:lust aboute this time of the year the House of Lords- would -h thrown. out the Franchise- Bill a eccond thus. Al a Liberal he was content to leave the matter to history, for he had very little deubt that history woald re- port that the new Franchise Bill was passed by Mr. (3-had- stone and his Government. He hail little doubt, however, that tiee Liberals. in every town and in every district in the existing division, would, as they tee,l done heretofore, continue to. use all their efforts in order that the country Inigh: have at its, head a Govern- ment of right and justice, a Government of economy, one that would develop and treceurege our trade and resources by just and honourable means, and one that would legislate not for any particular class in the coentry but for the goad of the we:ale country. (Applause.) Mr. T. Beeay, who was. reeeivel with hearty applause, began his speech by congratulating the meeting on the peeling of the Franchise Bill, which was, be said, not only 1 a great gin to the Liberal party, but a gain to ;he country at lere,-e—(hear, he are—for he felt sure that hint gy would show that the extension of the franchise had been a benefit ene a blessing. (Applauee.) If we estimated its probable effect by what followed the passing of the last Reform Bill, and the immerse strides in prosperity and influence which this c:untry had enjeyea since then, we might not unrea- eonably suppose that we were at the beginning of a new epoch which would show a great advance on the past. (Ap- ' plauee ) He felt a little bit doubtful with regard to the Redistribution Bill, no far as he understood it at present. To his mind it seemed that two members for each division would have been more likely to meet the wants of the eleeeors. (Hear, hear.) Thara must be in the minds of two men more knowledge thah there was in the mind 0 one man ; moreover a men who was sent to Parliament for the east time would feel at a disadvantage if he had no col- league in the representation of the district for which he himself had been returned. (Hew, bear.) In consenting to became a candidate for the representation of part of Che- shire the chief consideration which inflaenced him was a desire to bra fir the agricultural interest. (Applause) Hitherto that interest had had very little help from Parlia- ment generally. It was represented by very few men who hat really at heart the interests of agriculture. There were a bergs number of men in the House of Commons who had the interests of the owners of land at heart, but there was not a very large number who had the true interests of farmers at heart. (Hear, bear.) He should not have ac- cepted the invitation to contest that division if he had not be loved that an :: raenel.aer of Parllateent he would be better aele tonesee the Interests of the farmers than he could in aree ether position. (Applause.) He hoped, if elected, he Imight be able to do something towards obtaining security of tenwe for tenant farmers. (Renewed applause ) Three veers age he , xpte aced the opinion, at Altrincham, that the time had come when landlords should ii quire wheth'r it was not their duty to reduce the rents of their holdiega in very many cases. There had been large concessions and large percentages of rent retained to farmers for Some yeaLa That was all very well in its way, but it struck him that it would add very much he the enterprise of tenant farmers if rents were reduced permanently, and if they could be made to feel certain of realising the results of their own works and of securing not simply what was necessary to meet the wants of themselves and their families, but of being able to lay aside something for adverse times. (Applause.) There was no hope of securing any relief from the depression under which agriculture was now labouring by anything like a corn duty. (Applause.) Whatever might corns about he trusted we should not retrace our steps half a yard from that development of the Free Trade system which had been a great source of prosperity to this country. (Ap- plause.) He was amszed that politicians of any school shauld think that the proposal to reimpose a duty on corn would be listened to for a moment by the people at large, for a duty of that kind would be tantamount to a reduction in the wages of the working-classes, who would be quick to see that. There would, ha felt sure, be such a cacided anewee le the negetive to that proposal on the part of the new e!ecioial that it would at onee be nen thet no dRI7 on wheat or flout Would ever be tolerated in tilie eeuntry. (Applause) Mr. LEADAM, who was heartily received, remarked that General Gordon had been captured or slain several times over by Conservative newspapers and speakers, but from the intelligence which appeared in the newspapers that morn- ing it seemed that instead of Gordon being killed the Mehdi himself was almost " dried up." (Laughter.) . Liberals had been constantly confronted be accusations charging the Government with mal-administration in Egypt. Conserve- fives seemed to forget that when a child was learning to walk it was inevitable that the chili would fall occasion- ally. And while we are attempting to attune Oriental methods to European hartnonies we ought not to feel sur- prised if the official-s employed in the administration of Egypt incurred grieVons falls. Unless the people of this country were determined to abandon the policy of restoring, in time, a tranquilised and improved Egypt to the care of the Rzyptian people, and were determined insana to rate Egypt at the point of the sword, they must make up their minds that things would not go as smoothly a; otherwise one might desire. Supposing England were forgetful of her pledgee to Europe, to assert the right and power of the man in possession, and impose upon the reluctant Egyptian pepulatien an army of zealous and capable officials, alien from the people of Egypt in sympathy, the effect of that would be—allowing for the difference between Oriental and Western temperament—very much like what the effect upon the people of this country would be if an attempt werp made to impose the rigid and cast iron Prussian bureaucracy upoe them. If, therefore, the electors of England decided to adopt that alternative policy which was suggested ley many Conservatives, they must be prepared largely to in- crease the army in order that there might be permanently in Egypt from thirty to fifty thousand English soldiers. To do that they woull have tci put their hands deep into their pockets to pay the increased burden 0 taxation. (Hear, hear, and applause) At the conclusion of Mr. Leadem's speech two questions were put to him and to Mr. Rigby. The first asked if they ' were prepared to vote for the disestablishment of the Church of England, and the second whether they would vote for local option ?—Mr. LeAnene, in reply to the first question, repeated the answer he gave at a meeting held in the same room a short time ago.—xr. RIGBY said he would gladly vote for the disestablishment of the Church of England, mei should do so on the thee opportunity—(applause)—not from a wish to see that church destroyed, but from a desire to see it made more effective for geed. Both candidates ex- I pressed themselves favourable to the principle of local option, but iutimated that they did not think the country was, as yet, prepared to see that principle carried out by legislation. Mr. Lead= also said that it seemed to him— local option being passed as a principle—there should be limitations as to the maximum and minimum number of public-houses in a district. He did notghink the advocates of local option would pass through the House of Commons, and certainly not through the House of Lords, a local option bill by which any district would be absolutely pro- hibited from selling the smallest quantity of drink. The friends of local option must take what they could get, and have the minimum put as low as possible. Mr. T. W. He stated that in his opinion England had never known no good a Government as the one it now possesses. (Loud applause.)

TUE NEW CIIIMITEITT FOR EARLESTOWN —The new cemetery for Earleetown and Newton is ap- proaching completion, and the work is being,pushed on as rapidly as possible. The ground has all been laid out, and is being planted with trees, shrubs, and plants under the directions oe Mr. John Holmes, of Lawton. A delay has been occasioned in the erection of the chapel, but the lodge, in which ths gardener and keeper of the cemetery will reside, has been finished, and Mr. John Kettle, of Tarvin near Chester. who has been appointed to the post by the Newton Commissioners, took possession of the house on Thursday, last week. Since , then he leas resided on the premises. A RUNAWAY CAPTURED —OD the Bth September,, 18S2, Luke Doyle, a labourer, who then resided at Newton,. , was- summoned to appear at the Newton Petty Sessions to answer a charge of being drunk and disorderly on the 27. th of the previous month. The man;however, absconded, and I failed to appear at the Sessions. A warrant for his appre- hension was issued, but nothing further was heard of him until ten o'clock on Saturday night, when P.C. Spenceeap- , prehended him at Newton. The prisoner had apparently been away from ths town, and when seen by the constable , he was staying in an old haih3ing. ROBBERY IN NEWION HOLLOWS —On Wednesday night Elizabeth Clayton, single woman, in the employ of Messrs. Parr and Hunt, coal dealers, Gol horns, was return- ing with an empty cart and bores to Golborne from Newton, when she was met in the "Hollows "soon after dark by four strange men. She was asked if she had any money, and, replying in the negative, one man said be did not believe her, as women were seldom without. They allowed her to pass, but turned again upon her and began searching her clothing, her arms being firmly held behind her during the process. As the woman's screams were unheard the men continued the search until their object was attained, 14s. and some otti coppers baing found in an insiee pocket. This they quickly appropriated, and without attempting further injury quickly made off with their booty, which was all the woman possessed. SANITARY IMPROVEMENTS AT WAEGRAVE.

proveinents of an extensive character affecting the sanitary ' and sdwerage arrangements of the Wargrave district have recently been commenced, and the completion of the works should give satisfaction to the property owners as well as the inhabitant ef that neighhourbood, The whole of War- grave, from the Sunbeani Inn on One t WargraVe Church on the other side, will be thoroughly sewered and the road improved, while Park-road, from its junction with Wargrave-roed to below the new cemetery, will also be sewerediend improved, and in certain places widened. The work has been commenced as far as Park-road is concerned, and in consequence for some time to come the road will be impassable for conveyances and vehicles. The intended improvements are looked upon as being of a very necessary character. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT CROFT BOARD SCHOOL—The annual prize distribution and entertainment took place at the above school on Friday evening, under the patronage and in the presence of the members of the School Board. The schoolroom, which had neon tastefully decorated for the oc- casion, was crowded to its utmost capac'ty, and the Rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkham, MA , prgsided. A platform had been erected, on which upwards of fifty of the elder scholars were seated. After a few appropriate remarks by the Chair- man, a programme of songs, recitations, Szc, was rendered by the children, under the conductorship of Mr. Ball, the headmaster. At the conclusion of the entertainment, which was a most enjoyable one, the Chairman distributed the pritse to the schelars, after which Mr. Ball prop-ssd a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, and the proceedings terminated. SINGULAR MI HAP TO A LADY.—It ha, been truth- fully remarked that "accidents will happen," however careful one may be. A curious accident has recently hap, pened within a distance—say, of 100 miles—of Eerleatown, the details of which are of a peculiarly interesting charac- ter—to one person, at least. That person is a lady, young in years and fair in feitures. A short time ago Mi 93 well, we will refrain mentioning her name for obvious reasons, accompanied by one or two young lady c,mpacions, bad the privilege of being shown through a certain works where locomotion is the chief feature, and which are known 1 by a aarne symbolical of a he tthen deity, the god of subter- I raneons fires. As the fair ones proceeded on their tour of inspection, some bustle, in fact, a very unexpected and un- looked for bustle was plainly visible in one of the depart- ; ments throagh which the ladies passed. Happily neither the young lady nor her companions manifested any concern at to the excitement and "bustle" they had left behind them, but as for the workmen, it is stated they have not yet got over it.
