GOOD TEMPLIAIIISM AT EARLESTOWN.—Ou Saturday' evening a Degree meeting in connection with the Flops of , Earlestown lodge of Geed Templars was held in the lodge room, Bridge-street. The 3-d degree was conferred on five, candidates by Brother John Warburton, L.D., who was as- sisted by other lodge officers. The 2nd degree wart ease- quently canferred on seven other candidates. Afterwardsl a public entertainment was held under the presidency of 1 Brother John Taylor,' W.C.T. The room was well filled, and the proceedings were of a very enjoyable character, Songs were given by Brothers J. McDonald, Vint (Ashton), McKenzie, S. Rathbone (Ashten) ; readings by Brothers E. Newman, John Taylor, W. Walton, and Geotge Clarke el recitations by Sister Barnard, Brother Wm. Crampton, I Brother John Clarke; and selections of instrumental music by Mr. John Tripp (violin) and Brother Joseph James (dul- cimer). A duet by Sisters E. and J. Clarke was meets, given. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the entertainers on the-motion of Brother George Clarke, seconded by Brother George Warburton.—The usual weekly session of the lodge was held on Monday evening, when Brother John Taylor presided, and there was a large at- tendance. THS NEWTON COADDS9IONERS AND THEIR ROADS—In the Court of Appeal, on Thursday, before the Master of the Rolls and Lords Juetices Cotton and Lindley, a case was heard in reference to the Wigan and Warrington turnpike- road, being the appeal of the defendants in the case of the Improvement Commissioners for Newton-in-Makerfild e. -Justices of the County Palatine of Lancaster against the judgment of the Queen's Bench Division on a special case. Mr. Gorst, Q C., appeared for the appellants, and Mr. Charles, Q.C., for the respondents. The special case set out that the plaintiffs were incorporated by the Newton District Improvement Act of 1885, which statute embodied the Towns Improvement Clauses Act of 1847. The Newton district was traversed by what was formerly a . turnpike read, leading from Wigan to Warrington, and upon the passage of the Act of 1855 the maintenance of that and all other roads in the dis- trict became vested in the commissioners, and the trustees of the turnpike ceased to repair it within the limits of the district. The Warrington and Wigan turnpike trust expired in 1877. The Highways Locomotives Act provided that any road wkich had within the period between the 31st Dec., 1870, and the date of the passing of the Act ceaeed to be a turnpike road, or should afterwards cease to be such, should be deemed to be a main road, and one-half of the expenses incurred in repairing it should he paid by the county au- thorities. ?All the proper conditions bad been satisfied so as to enable the Improvement Commissioners to receive from the county the expense necessary for repairing the road for the period for which their claim was brought A divisional court gave judgment in favour of the plaintiffs on this special case, and against their decision the defend- ants now appealed. Judgment was reserved. A MADMAN AT EARERSTOWN: EXTRAORDINARY Con- DUCT—About a quarter to 11 o'clock on Thursday week, some of the inhabitants of Market-street, Earlesto en, were astonished by the appeirance in the streets of a man without shoes, coat, or hat, who appeared to be engaged irk training for pedestrian contests, or running races with an imaginary rival. From his wild looks, however, certain people sate mined that the individual was of unsound mind, and the at- tention of P.C. Hunt was called to his strange behaviour. The constable took him to the Eerlestown police station, where he gave the name of Winfield Warwick, and stated that he resided at 4, Derby-street, Mamie, Cheshire. Ile was subsequently examined by Dr. Patterson, of Earles- town, who pronounced him to be insane. The Man was placed in one of the cells, and was attended during the night by the constables. Abou', three o'clock on the follow- ing morning the extraordinary conduct of the prisoner geve.rise to an exciting scene. At the time mentioned ti e lunatic stated that he was hungry, arid P.O. Lloyd accon!- __

ingly left the cell to procure -hirit something to eat. A few moments afterwards P.C. Lloyd heard a smash, but when he returned to the door of the cell everything was quiet. The ofilcsr handed ths food through a mill aper- ture in the door, and called upon the man to take it, but the reply he got was a treacl,erons and violent blow on his hand with a lump of wood, which afterwards turned out to b. the cover of an article in the cell. This cover lyid been fastened with a lock and iron bars, but the prisoner had forcibly wrenched it away. With this weapon he battered the cell door and made several dents about an inch deep in the sheet iron with which the door was lined. The con- stable thereupon called for the assistance of P,Cds Parker

'and Hunt, andsa desperate struggle with the man ensued By the united exertions of the three constableo he was at length secured, and was kept safe until the forenoon, when he was removed to Newton, and where he was examined by Dr. J. W. Watlsins, medical officer of healthh for the district. He was afterwards taken bore Mr. T. J. Gillespie, J.P., at the Newton Town Hall, and was charged with being a lunatic wandaring at large. He was orderei to be removed to an asylum. /a the afternoon he was conveyed to Rain. hill Asylum.

TILE SCARLET FEVER EPIDEMIC AT EARLES- TOW N.—N4 ORE DETffa Notwithstanding every effort on the part of the local authorities, the epidemic of scarlet fever at Earles- town still remains of a serious character, and is caus- ing some uneasiness in the district. During the last few days there have been seven or eight new cases reported, and there have been four deaths--the neighbourhoods affected being Earle-street and Booth-street. The authorities are doing theinutmost to repel the attacks of the unwelcome visitant, and with the view of disseminating information upon the subject a large number of placards have been circulated.; in the township, giving precautions against scarlatina,. and containing suggestions, for preventing the spread of infectious or contagious diseases of any nature. I FEARF7C,LE SUDDEN DEATH OF A laturnaß AND SISTER.

The suddenness of the attacks of infectious disease and the rapidity with which death has followed in severwl in- stanceAuring the present epidemic,: of scarlet fever in Earlestown, has given rise to considerable sympathy ter the suffering persons and sorrowing relatives, but an unusually painful event has occurred during the present week. On Saturday last Ann Vaudrey, a ne-looking young woman of 17". years, residing at 1.94, Earle-street, with other rela- tions, attended the funeral of an aunt at War- grave Church, and was thee apparently in the best of health. On the Sunday she attended the customary services at church, but on the Monday she complained of illness. She rapidly grew worse, and not- withstandirg the attentions of Dr. J. N. Patterson, who was called in, she expired at nine o'cl ck on the following Wednesday morning—it is supposed from scarlet fever. This untimely end of the young woman was a sad blow to her parents and friends; but still the trouble did not end here. Up to the commencement of the present week Thomas Vaudrey, 19 years of :gra (brother of the deceased young woman), who was employed as a turner at the Viaduct Works, had not complained of any illness, but about 11 o'clock on Tuesday forenoon he was compelled to leave his work and return home. He was also attended by Dr. Pat- terson, but, as in the case of his deceased sister, he soon succumbed to his illness, which terminated fatally about four o'clock on Thursday afternoon. This unlooked for double sudden death in one house has cast quite a gloom over the neighbourhood, and many expressions of syrapatki for the unfortunate family have been expressed.
THE FRAUDS ON EARLESFOWN TRADESMEN. OVER 50 PERSO.I9 DOPED.

At the Occasional Court House, Warrington, on Wednes- day, before Mr. James Mame, the married worn in named Sarah Ann Wallace Mehra Haskins, residing in Rethbone- street, Earlestown, was agein charged on remand with hav- ing at Earleatown on the 28tta October, obtained the sum of Sc by false pretences from Benjamin Kelly, tobacconist, Queen-street. She was further charged with obtaining in a similar manner, the sum of Is, from Tom Ambergete Bell, picture dealer, Haydock-street, Earlestown ; and also the sum of 3e 6:1 from Robert Pugh,furniture dealer, Bridge. street, Earlestown. The evidence, which was previously given, was repeated, and P.S. Commins in reply to the Bench ,who asked if anything was known about her, and how long she had carried on such practices, said there were over 50 shopkeepers and tradesmen in Earlestown who bad been victimised by the prisoner in a similar manner. She was then committed for trial at the next quarter sessions at Liyerpeol, upon each of the three chargee mentioned. It may be added that the inquiries which the police have Made in the previOns conduct 101 transactiens of oc2;:i.. sonar, shove that her prodeedingt4 halm been Conducted Ole an extensive scale. On the authority of P.S. Commins, who deserves every praise for the energetic manner in which the case was completed, we are assured that over 50 similar charges could be preferred against the women, Generally her mode of procedure was to call on a certain tradesman and represent that she was a person of a different name to her real name, adding that she lived in a district quite away from her proper residence. Sometimes she gave leer ad- dress as the Vulcan, other times as Newton, and occasion- ally as near the Viaduct, at the far end of Earle-street, whereas her house was in Rathbone-street. To obtain sums of money she gave various stories. She had either been purchasing groceries or drapery and had forgot her purse, or her husband was a customer of the party from whom she was seeking to obtain the money. So precise was her story that she mentioned the hour at which the money should ha returned, but subsequent inquiries realised the fact that she was not the person she had repreeented herself to be, and that she did not reside at the address she gave. In one case she obtained 2e from a tradesman by representing that her father was dead at Manchester and she wanted to bor- row the sum named to pay her fare to Manchester so that she could see his body before interment. To give some show of truth to her statement she held in her hand a tele- graph form which she said was the message containing the sad news. In another case she exhibited a letter which she stated was from her relations staring that her father was dead, and by this story she obtained 2s from the daughter of a reverend gentleman resident in Earlestown. To the wife of a medical gentleman in Earlestown she also represented that her father was dead and thereby ob- tained 4s 6d.
PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR AT EARLESTOWN.

With the obiect of clearing off a portion of the debt on the new schools, erected by the Primitive Methodists in Lord-streez, off L.gh•street, Earlesto am. a three days' baz tar and stole of work was opened on Thursday afternoon by Mr. William P. Hartley, of Southport. The erection of the schools supplied a longfeft want, and with the commo- dious premises they have now at their disposal the Primi- tive Methodists of Earlestown and district confidently hope that they will be able to carry on their mission and school work more satisfactorily and with a, greater degree of suc- cess. The total cost of the schools was 1:800, and towards this amount over £3OO have been raised. By the present effJrt it is hoped that about £2OO will be realised. The room was attractively decorated under the directions of Messrs Evans and McClure, who kindly carried out that work gratuitously. Numerous banners and mottoes were displayed in prominent positions, at one end of the school being a splendid silk banner, bearing the words " E town Primitive Methodist Sabbath School" in gold letters on a blue around.

The stalls were four in number—two on each side of the room—and were filled with articles of the iniscellaneons character usually found at such gatherings: Tha first stall contained anti-macassars, children's clothing, cushione, toilet mats, slippers, fancy boxes, dm, and was in charge of Mrs. T. Clarke, Mrs. P. Thompson, Mrs. J. Bagnal!, Mrs. T. Holleyock, Mrs. W. Warden, Mrs. R. Sproston, and Mrs. T. Dean. Dio. 2 stall was well filled with an assortment of cushions, anti-micassars, fancy slippers, ebildren'S toys crockery, a splendid Urns-piece, and a box of cigars, and was entrusted to the care of Mrs. Austin, Mrs. C. Pendrey,. Mrs. T. Jackson, Mrs. T. Worsley, Ms. J. Sproston,.Mrs. W. Austin, Mrs. Kemp, and Mrs. Berry, The chief %attires of No. D, stall were articles of a similar character to the two preceding stalls. The ladies in charge were Mrs. T. Woods, Mrs. S. Arrowsinith, Mrs. W. Banton, Mrs. J. Tombs, Mrs. J.:Pierce, Mrs. E. Dickens, and Mrs. C. Watson. The fourth stall was none behind the other stalls is its at- tractive display of miscellaneous articles, and it was looked after by Mrs. T. Worsley (Wargrave House), Mrs. W. Worslev, Mrs. J. Worsley (Vitriol-square), Mrs. J. Worsley (Newton-terrace), and Miss E. Worsley (Wargrave House). In addition there was a refreshment stall in charge of Mies Clarke • an interesting " curiosity shop "under the manage- ment of Mr. J. Bagnall ; and a comparatively excellent "art gallery" presided over by Mr. T. Ormanct. The art gallery WAS one of the features of te bazaar, and contained a series of views, paintings in oil and water colours, etch- ings, sketches, and photographs lent by various friends, including Mr. Ashton, Mr. Bradshaw, Mr. E. Jones, Mr. Ormand, and Mr. Gowanlock. Among the exhibits were , winks by local artists, amongst whom might be mentioned Mr. Ewan R. Jones, Mr. Henry Brddslaw, Miss Thsmpson, and Mr. G.. Blair.

At the opening ceremony there was a very large atten- dance, among those present being the Revs. F. N. Shimmin (residsnt rninster), J. M. Fairbourne (Wesleyan), and W. C. Tayler (Baptist), Messrs. P. Chandley, C. Ashton, T. Ormand, T. Clark, Bagnall, Burchall, and Dickens. The Rev.F. N. Shimmin presided, and in stating the object of the bazaar said that the movement with which it was as- sociated was started something like five years ago. It was felt they wanted better chapel and school accommodation, but as to which they should have first, was a matter far further consideration. Sometimes they had been cast down and sometimes there had been streaks of cheering light, and people had wondered whether or not they would ever suc- ceed in accomplishing their desires. The present bazaar did not fully represent the labours of their lady friends, many of whom had silently and earnestly worked in connection with the sewing meeting, and certain sums of. money they had raised the treasurer had placed to their credit. Sinse July last they had appealed to the public for help, and for a town like Earlestown he thought they had raised a very largo sum of money. He was pleased ta see that notwithstanding everything that had been done that bazaar promised to be a decided SIMMS. They had in their Sunday School about 300 scholars, and about 100 met in a Band ef Hops. They hoped to increase the number by hard work ani fair means, for now they had accommodation for 500 in that room, where there was plenty of space, good ventilation, excellent light, five good class-rooms, a library, and an infants' MOM. The building had cost over £BOO, and there was over £1043 yet to be raised. They hoped that amount would receive its death blow by the pre.ent effort, and he was glad to introduce to them to open the bazaar a gentleman who sympathised with them, and who had promised to give them 10 per cent. on the amount they raised. (Applause.) He thought it was an excellent offer, and was an inducement for them to work hard. If they raise 3 £2OO or £3OO it would place them in a very easy position, and they would not have put up a build- ing which would crush their church. He thought they could honestly meet their liabilities, and do a good work in Earlestown without treading on the corns of any church or chapel in the neighbourhood. (Applaase.)—Mr. W. I*. Hartley, on rising to declare the bersar open, was received with hearty applause. In a lengthy address he anted that that was his first visit to EArlestown, awl he was

very much pleased to see their new school, their ob.:.ent. building which was to teach the rising race the principles of religion. Mt they had heard there was over £40() yet to be raised to clear it from debt, and he thought that if the members of the Church of Christ and its adherents realised the responsibilities a beamr like that would not have been necessary. Hit advocated a systematic giving to the funds of the church, and held that the spasmodic efforts to raise money for a Christian Church were contrary to the prin- ciples of Caristianity. He concluded by declaring the bazaar open, (applause.),--On the motion of the Rkvs J. M Fairbourno, seconded by the Rev. W. C. Tayler,..who condemned the practice of raffling at bazaars, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Bgr. Hartley, who briefly acknow- ledged the complirnen%. and business was at once com- menced.

IMPORTANT LOCAL COLLIERY CASE.. LORD GBRARD V. BROMILOW. At the sitting of the Chancery Court of the County. Pal- atine at St. George's Hall, Liverpool, on Thursday week, a case which involved some important points affecting euelliery leases was oommenced.—Mr. Rotch appeared for the plain- tiff, and M. Neville for the defendant.—Mr. Roteh stated that the real qeestion. in the case Was as to the construc- tion of a certain agreement. On the let of Janeery, 1655, the plalutiff demised to the defendant the right of working certain epacified seams of coal on the Garswood Park Farm, of 85 acres, and some adjoining land, fora term of,..years. at a certain specified rental; but it was especially provided and agreed that if before the expiration of the lease the whole of the merchantable coal in the thereby. demised mines cliould have been paid for and got, then the said lease or term of 35 yeare should cease and determine at the end of the-then current year in the saute manner c.a.ieeit had eot- pired by effiuxion of time. In July, 1883, the defendant paid for the remainder, or estimated remainder of the un- wcrked coal, and the effect of that was he ceased to have any further liability whatever in respect of the dead rents and.footage rents. The legal effect of their.paying for this coal before they had actually obtained it might be a ques- tion in the oase.—Mr. Neville: We say that the coal is paid for and gotten, and the mine done and filled up—Mr.l Retch : And we say that merchantablecoal, in considerable quantity—at least 500 tons—remains;, and if so, we eontend that the lease remains in force. He added that the next phase of the case depended upon an agreement of the 5.h of October, 1876, under which the defendant proceeded to work another and separate coal area known as Laffak Gars- wood ; and in that agreement certain things were to be done and observed according to the useal clauses in Lord Ger- ard's leases. Tne defendant continued working both toe mines till the let of July, 18e3; and then they stopped working at both Garswood Park and leaflet& Garswood, and claimed that both lease and agreement were at an end. The plaintiff stow asked for specific performance. He read the agreement, and arguel that upon a reasonable construction of it there was nothing to entitle the defen- dents to treat the two collieries as one concern under the lease of 1855, so that even assuming the defendants' action was right as to Garswood Park Colliery, they were wrong as to Laffak Garswood, where there was admittedly a large quantity of ungotten coal. They had raised £60,000 worth of coal there, but it had not paid well. At Garswood Park, however, the defendants had made a large fortune.—The Vice Chancellor said it appeared to him that if a lease were granted for any term, and after that an agreement referring to the lease were arrived at, the same conditions as those of the original lease would attach, and fulfilment of the condi- tions of the orkinal lease would determine the whole.—Mr. Rotch repeated that the phrase in the agreement was the usual conditions of Lord Crerard's leases, whereas the condi- tions of the 1853 lease were special and not usual ; and if the defendants had wis ed for the conditions of that special lease they should have made a bargain to that effect —The Vice Chancellor said that this was an agreement for a lease only and not a concluded document, and therefore the court was justified by all the authorities in hesitating to direct specific performance.—Mr. Rotch said that there had been some years of part performance.—The Vice Chancellor ad- mitted.the force of part performauce, hut in this case it ap- peered to be entirely eoeeleient with the defendant's view, —Evidence was then called,after which the court adjourned to Monday, when the hearing was continded.-Mr, Laurence summed up the case for the defence, and contended that upon a reasonable interpretation the leases of both collieries were determined on the Ist of July, 1883.—Mr. Rotch re- plied, contending that, the defendants had failed to show that they had taken out the whole of the workable coal, as pro. tided in the team before the tenancy could cease. He also submitted that his evidence showed that a substantial quantity of coal still remained unwotked.— On Tuesd ty, the Vice-Chaneellor, ire delivering judgment, said that this was a case in which, if he had any difficulty about it, it was requisite he should take time to consider his judgment. It was certainly a difficult case, but he should, however, do no more than justice in giving his judgment at once if his mind was deer upon it. The point was one of considerable importance, both for the plaintiff and the de- fendant. On the one hand if the plaintiff was right he was entitled to a sum of at least £6,000 ; on the other hand, if the defendant was right he was entitled to be released from making that payment. The evidence left it to his mini that there was still under the Garswood Mine coal which could have been got, but not gotten, was paid for. Ile therefore came to the conclusion that the plaintiff was en- titled to have the specific terms of the agreement fulfilled. In the ordinary course of jedgment he should have given to the phintiff the costs of successful litigation. But here he was under a difficulty of finding. So much uncertainty had been caused by the way in which the matter in the first instance was dealt with by the plaintiff himself and his agents that he did not think it was a case to give costs against the defendants. Both parties would pay their own costB.

ODDFELLOWSHIP.—On Saturday the monthly meeting of the Triumphant Lodge, Independent Order of Oddfelloyes, M.U,, Friendly Society, took place at the Gerard Arms Hotel. There was a very good attendance of members. The customary business of the lodge leaving been disposed of a new member was initiated and a delegate appointed to represent the lodge at the next district meeting to be held on the 27th inst. at Ashton. The propositions for the various lodge offices were again taken, with the result that the offices of lodge surgeon., sick visitor, and elective secretary are likely to be contested. The secretary then read the accounts and the minutes of the evening, and the lodge was closed in the usual manner.

PARK-LANE PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—On Frlday night the house was so over-crowded that some 20 persons had to go away, not being able to get admission to bear a debate on the following subject, viz. That this house is 3f opinion that the hereditary House of Peers is an unnecessary, cumberous, and obstructive institution, and as such ought to be abolished with the utmost despatch." The resolution was most ably moved by the member for Ashton- tinder-Lyre. The following members took part in the debate :—Woodstock, Wigan, Taunton, Blackburn, Lincoln, Prime Minister, Liverpool and Derby. The Speaker's decision for the ayes was challenged, and the division was taken with only one of a majority in favour of the ayes.

div.p: GOLBORNE.

SERVICE OF SONG.—The very pmular service of song, entitled "Poor Mike," was given tr:.fore a crowded congre- gation in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Lowton-read, last Sunday night. The Rev. T. Vaughan proved an ac- ceptable reader; the chair being occupied by Mr. Glover. The service was a great success; the proceeds were in aid of the society funds -

Gousonxii Litatzar, CLria —The Golborne Liberal Club has proved itself unusually attractive this week on account of an extensive bagatelle handicap having been set on foot by the committee. Tkere are 26 competitors, each of whom will have to play together before the result is known. The first prize (presented by William Mitchell, Eslt.), is a case of birds, and the second prize will probably be a goose.

ACCIDENT.—James Flinn, 18, residing at kligh•street, Golborne, and employed in the carding department of Messrs. S. Brewis and Co's.,. Old Mill, met with a serious Sc. cident on Saturday whilst at work-. His arm got fast in one of the straps, the result being that his head and face was dragged into the machinery. His jaw bone was broken, four of his teeth were knocked out, and his face badly cat.

A NEW FIRE BRIOADE.—Last Saturday afternoon the new fire engine which has been put down by Messrs. Smithson Brothers at their Golborne mill was tested in the presence of the head of the firm and Mr. Holism, general d manager. A large volume of water was carrie right over the mill, and it is calculated that under favourable circumstances the new mill brigade will be able to couple up and get the hose at work within one minute from the time afire may be announcEd. WESLEYAN METHODISM.—The Golborne West ayans held a meeting on Thursday night to consider what stens ought to be taken to secure the two-fold object of pewing the present chapel and building a Sunday school. It was stated that some time ago a number of subscriptions were pro- mised and an effort was made to call the unpaid amounts in. In the meantime weekly donations had been paid. After some discussion it was agreed to ask that the balance be paid within a given period. The feeling of the meeting was then taken as to the advisability of holding a basaae in tronnection with the scheme, and itwas unanimously decided to inaugurate oste as soon as the necessary arrangements could be made. A series of lectures are contemplated.

div.head: PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.

- A meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday afternoon, at the Parochial Office, Go'borne, Mr. W. Mit- shell presiding, and there being also present Messrs. T. Mitchell, J. Taylor, Arnott, Pierpoint, Femme, Garton, and Yates, and Mr. Bennie (clerk and surveyor).—The Surveyor reported that he had received. a letter from Mr. Williams stating that at a meeting of the Leigh Rural Sanitary Authority on the 20th ult., &resolution was passed that he (the surveyor) be instructed to see that the refuse left by persons who emptied astipito in Go!borne be removed as early as possible; he bad not yet, however, had an opportu- nity of attending to the matter. The macadam had been stripped off the road near Brick Bridge, and the work of lifting the declivity was progressing favourably. In the ceurse of slew days the whole of the macadamised roads in the township would have been repaired with broken stone, and he esked permission to hire a steam roller for two days far work in the township. He estimated the cost of laying, a water main from Bank Heath, down Barn-lane, to the end of Legh-street, at £7O. To lay a main of about 150 ,yards in length, so as to enable a supply to be conveyed to ilighfield House would cost about £23. On the 11th April be reported several old standing encroachments on the highways in the township which had not been considered. The one in front of the Old Heywoode had been renewed contrary to his request. The ditches in Newton. Hollows and Edge Green- lane required cleaning, and as they were the property of the township, he desired instructions to take the work in hand. The consumption of water for the past month was 1,064,000 gallons. Having perused the Awerd on frequent occasions to make himself familiar with the fghts a the town- ship, he had formed the opinion that the mines and minerals Leader many of the highways belonged to the township. He suggeeted that counsel's opinion should be taken on the question.—A conversation on the various matters referred to in the report followed.—The Surveyor was instructed to hire a steam roller, it was de- cided to take what action mowed most advisable in respect to the encroachments complained of, and the question of a watermain being laid to lEglefield House was deferred for future consideration, as was also the suggestion of the sur- veyor that counsel's opl,sion should be taken on the right of the township to the mines and minerals under the roads. —A. discussion took place with reference to the use of water, and the Survovor expressed the opinion that it was ' being extravagantly used.—Mr. Garton suggested that the water should be cut off at six o'clock in the evening until the same hour next mailing, as a test of what might be supposed to run to waste.—lt was decided that notices cautioning people against wasting water ehould he issued, Mr. Bennie stating %hat offendere were liahte 14 A penalty not exceeding .410‘

A friend called upon Heine the poet a few days before his death. Said Heine, "You will find me dull and stupid this morning. U. Choa has been with me" (M. Choa was a notorious blockhead), "and we changed our minds." Too EARLY rou MiscntsF.—A newly-married couple riding in a carriage were overturned, whereupon a bystan- der said it was "a shocking sicht." " Yes," said the gentleman—" to see those just wedded fall out so soon !" "Papa, what do you intend to give me for a birthday pre' sent?" asked a young girl of her father, a well•known Lon- don magistrate. "Give you," said the magistrate, whose mind was evidently on something else—"give you? I'll give you six months." An old lawyer, in examining a witness who had been in the Army, said, "Come, soldier—tell us what you know of this matter." "lam no soldier—l am an officer," haughtily replied the witness ; whereupon the old lawyer said calmly, "Well, then, officer who is no soldier, tell us what you know,"
GOOD ADVICE.—On one oonAon a friend of Lord Alvanley's, came for hl3 advice in the. following circum-

stances. "'Mr. has threatened to kick me whenever he sees me in society. What am I to do if he comes into the room?' Mt down,' replied Lord Alvanley."—Lord Ifalmesbury's Memoirs. 'AT AND 'ED.--:The late Thomas Carlyle undonMedly _

possessed the popular homage. A stranger on the box of an omnibus' seeing the historian get in, observed that the "old fellow" had " a queer 'at." " Queer 'at !" answered the driver. "As', he may wear a queer 'at; but what would you give for the 'ed-piece, that's inside of it ?" Archbishop Whately was once accosted at the table of the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland by an aide•de-camp, with the question, " What is the difference' your Grace, between an archbishop and a donkey ? " His Grace owned that he did not know. "The archbishop has a cross on his breast, and the donkey on his back.' " Yes, yes ; oh! I see ; very good. "And," added his Grace, "what is the diffe- rence between an aide-de-camp and a donkey." "I do not see any," was the unsuspecting reply. " Neither de I," said the archbishop. A Hibernian orator, dilating on the wrongs of his country, said that for a long series of years West of Ireland farmers had not only borne the vile Saxon oppression, but had to suffer also a severe "visitation of Providence," "A visita- tion of ireprovieence, he means," was the audible comment of an Dieter man who stood in the crowd. "This is a funny doctrine," exclaimed Brown, who had _ been reading of metempsychosis. "fhe idea of the human soul entering the body of an animal. According to this doctrine, my soul may, at some future time, inhabit the body of a jackass !" "And why not ?" demurely asked the friend who was listening. "It would certainly feel more at home there than anywhere else." ONE OF TEE GANG. A clergyman bought a pair of horses from a set of ropers in Brighton. When he had taken them horns and found them useless, he returned and com- plained bitterly to the landlord of the inn in whose stable, they had been standing. 6` Well, sir," the man said " any one could see they were copers, and I precious won got rid of them; but—you will excuse me, sir—you was so jail green I thought you must be one of the gang." Confectioner : "Remember that all the French sweets are in this case." New assistant: "flow do you get them fresh ?" Confectioner: "Why, we make them, of course !" Assistant : "But I thought French sweets were imported." Confectioner : "Oh, ho : we make them ourselves!" Assistant : "But, then, why are they oilier] French sweets ? Do the ingredients come from France ?" Confectioner : 'Well, I don't know; maybe the plaster of Paris does." PREPARING FOR BUSINESS.—" John," said a chemist, , "how is our stock of lint for b a:Wages?" "Got plenty," said John. "And arnica—are we well supplied with that?" "Yes, sir." "Our stock of salves, lotions, and broken-bone " remedies of all sorts is complete, is it ?" "Yes, sir; we've got enough of everything.' "Very well, then," said the proprietor, glancing at the sky through the front window ; " it locks as though we might have a cold freezing night, and you had better go out and wash down the steps!" LEARNING HIS TRADE —American editor: "-See here; you told me you had had experience as reporter." New man "Yes" "Then how does it happen that you use such unjournalistic languege as this—'The Hon. William Blank next addressed the meeting'?" "Isn't that aft • right ? " "All right! It's, all wrong! One would think the meeting was in favour of our own party! Why, sir, it's an opposition meeting ! " "I can't see what difference that makes. Hew should I write it ? " "Why, in this way— Bill Blank next harangued the crowd.'" • An amusing anecdote is recorded of the Princess Beatrice. It is said that, when a child of six or seven, she was ex- tremely pertinacious; an assertion which, if the following story be true, seems amply verified. It is well known that the late John Brown was a specially favourite servant of Her Majesty Queen Victoria. The Princess was in the habit of addressing him as "Brown." The Queen remonstrated with her and bade her for the future say "Mr. Brown." The next time she saw him the Princess again said "Brawn," and she was then told that if she disobeyed a second time she would be put to bed in puni-hment. Soon after this they met again, and the Princess .lost no time in walking up to him and saying, "How do you de, Brown ? I hope your're quite well, Brown? And now, good-night, eee Brown, for I'm going to bed, Brown." And she went. ThE MONSTER IN PERSON.—The fallowing anecdote, e, which appears in the Croker correspondence, supplies an s! amusing sequel to a well-known story. "Every one knows the story of a gentleman's asking Lord North who 'that , frightful woman was,' and his lordship's answering, That is my wife.' The other, to repair his blander, said, 'I did not mean her, but that monster next. to her.' 'Oh,' said Lord North, that monster is my daughter!' With this story Frederick Robinson, in his usual absent enthusiastic way, was one day entertaining a lady whom he sat next to at dinner, and, 10, the lady was Lady Charlotte; Lindsay— the monster in question ! " Many years ago the only inn at Keswick was called the "Cock," and was much frequented by the visitors to the Lake Districts. But, the late excellent Bishop of :Llandaffe Dr. Richard Watson, happening to reside in the neighbour- hood, and being universally eeteemed and loved, the land- lord, out of compliment to hie lordship, changed his sign to- the "Bishop's Head." Another inn was shortly after opened in the village, and fee proprietor selected the "Cock" as his sign. The landlord of the old inn, finding that the rival establielernent, owing to its name, threatened to deprive him of many of his cuetemers, in consequence of the guidee books recommending the " Cock " E. 3 the best inn, wrcte. under the bishop's head at his door,. "This is the original Old Cache"' to the great amusement of the bib'sop. •

WAGES,3N WEST Litycisurra.—A confer- ence was.held on Monday at Wigan between the Exuntive Committee of the West Lancashire Coal Association, con - Stating of 10 mcmbers an.l a like number of miners' dategates, reprmating the various districts in Weat Lan- cashire. The bitter submitted an agreement for a proposed eliding scale for the regulation ef miners' wages in. West Lancashire, which was read to the meeting by Mr, Thomas Ashton, miners' secretary. After some remarks by the delegatos on the poposed scale it was arranged that the meeting should- he adjourned until Monday the 2204 December, In ordor that the employers' committee might have an opportunity of considering the proposed sliding scale, and that prior to the adjourned meeting, Mr. Maskell Peace, on behalf of the eliplovers should submit to the miners' representatives a draft sliding scale in a form in which the employers' committee would he willing to agree to it, so that both aides might come to the adjourned meeting fully authorised and prepared to agree to a sliding so% agreement.

COMMERCE AND CO-OFERSITION.—A meeting of delegates from co-operative societies who are associated with the Co- operative Union was held on Saturday, lit Manchester, to _ present a testimonial to Mr. Thomas Hughes, Q.O ,as a mark of esteem for his long and valuable services to the , Co-operative cause, and his sacrifices on its account. A sum of £1,900 was subscribed for the testimonial. The greater part of this amount had been devoted to founding a scholarship at Oriel College, Ocfard, bearing Mr. Hughes's • name. A gold watch few Mr. Hughes and a casket of Jewel- lery for Mrs. Hughes were also taught, and these were for- mally presented on Saturday. Delegates attended the gathering from all parts of England, and also from Scot. • land. The Bishop of Manchester took the chair. Ma Hughes, in acknowledging the testimonial, spoke of the present crisis in England's commercial history. One uni- versal cry of distress was going up from every trade and industry in the land. And what wag that cry? "Too much corn," "too much sugar," "too much cotton," "toe much labour," too much, in short, of every species of wealth, and yet merchants and manufacturers were being ruined, while two-thirds at least of our people were underfed, badly clothed, and miserably housed. Free competition had been proclaimed as the sole adjuster of supp'y and demand—the mi-sacred law of trade—and so every man's hand had teen against his neighbour, until the keenest and least scrupulous, instead of the wisest and most upright men, had come to the front and got the control of almost every branch ' of industry and trade. He did not say that the time had actually come when an honest and scrupulous man could not live by trade, bat it was not far off. The coach would beeves the precipice before they knew it unless the .horses could be turned into the right road. How were they to be turned ? By a means familiar enough to them as co-opera- tors. Men must be fallow worker, not rivals; justice must rule trade. If They must have a single watchword, "Con- cert" was that word; concert must be set foot to foot against compel' ion in every department of human life, never to yield an inch, but to stand as for dear life till the battle was won. (Loud applause.) div.head: RAFFLES AT BAZAARS.
div.p: RAFFLES AT BAZAARS.

Sir,—Many of your readers have doubtless seen in the newspapers that the Watch Committee of the Birmingham Corporation have resolved to prosecute all persons taking part in ratii.s or lotteries, at bazaars; but I think it advis- able that clergymen and ministers Of religion should have notice that any bizsar promoter or stallholder permitting or committing such offences can be prosecuted by any person whatever, without the intervention of the Watch Cmunittee or any ether authority, and are consequently at ths mercy of anyone who may have personal feeling against them, or against the denomination to which they belong, or who may have a general objection to the law being broken, and thisliability continues for six months after the commis- sion of the offence. Very strong antagonism to bazaars as means of rasing money for religious purposes is manifes- tel by some, but others who bold different opinions should sorely not becerne law-breakers to further the objects they have in view. It is no argument to urge that the wrong- doing is for the purpose of obtaining money, and that for a good object ; the forger and embezzler commit offences to obtain money, and as for the object " the end does ;eat justify the means "—Your obedient servant, 11. B. WHITE.
Clerk to the Borough Magistrates, Warrington. P.B.—A person convicted of the above-named offences is liable to imprisonment for three months with herd labour as a rogoo and a vagabond.
TICKET PROSECUTIONS AND THE ST. lIELENS
BAZAAR.

Sir,—By what has recently transpired in the Borough Police Courts, we are famished with an evidence of the in- tentions of the police to put down plebeian betting and the sale of Connolly's and other lottery tickets. In view of our C 5 proximity to Christmas, the action on the part of the police will doubtless have a salutary check on the further development of "Christmas Draws," which may have been ia embryo. But whilst concluding that such will be the case, we may pardonably ask will the effects be as effica- cious in arresting the development of those other " Christ- mas Deaws," fashionably designated " Bazaars ? " Judging frona what occurred in the Town Hall within the last few days, we may safely assume that instead of a check being pnt to the progress of such bazaars, magisterial sanction will be given to these illegal lotteries by reason of names with J.P. appended, being publiehed in the list of patrons, and possibly some such dignitaries to open the affeir. And those erratic guardians ef the law— the police—will probably be represented by two of their number posing with stately mien to guard the portals of the edifice wherein the law they are sworn to maintain is being flagrantly breached. Now, while it was urgently necessary to put down Connolly's tickets, ..te , the promoters of these euphetni-ticelly termed " bazaars" are at the same time guilty of reprehensible conduct. In law there is no difference between a raffle at the "Pig and Whistle" and a lottery under mayoral patronage at the Town Hall ; or in the sale of Connolly's tickets by mine host of the " Flying Brick " and the sale of a ticket by a prominent tradesman for the disposal of an American organ at the Town Hall for the benefit of the building fund of St. Mark's Church. All ! alike are illegal, and if we view the matter from a moral standpoint the promoters of the bazaar in aid of St. Mark's Church stand in much less favourable positions, as by pre- ! cept and example their effects are widely pernicious; and if keetice is to be perverted as at present in aid of religion the resell will be the further alienation of the people from that ' church which proadly apes humility. The actuating motive of Connolly's ticket agents was to get money only, and this was alike the incentive that lea- polled the promoters of the late bazaar ;r1 the Town Hall. The positions of the two are further paralelled, as where the ; god Bacchus is essentially the patron and attraction to the ' publican's raffle so is St. Mark arrogated to the patronage of the church whilst they also wilfully break the laws of this CLristian country. But if the publicans' god Bacchus is neeless in defence of Boniface, it is not a with the church, ! as the Grundyistri of society provides fer her an all power- I fc.l, protection against the remit of her transgressions. It is this slavish pandering to Mrs. Grundy and its results which call to mind the doggerel lines— Since laws were made for every degree. To curb vi2e in others as well as in me, I wonder we hav'nt better companee On Tyburn tree. And which may be appropriately chorused by the late prits of the police court. - .

It is truly a cutting satire on the vaunted piety of a Christian Church—the richest in the world, having £40,000,000 sunk in property, when with all this wealth, it is found reduced to such miserable shifts to eke out the me ms necessary to build a place of worship. Evidently the god Mammon and the Golden Calf have devotees " within the fold to-day equally as numerous as those who gave Moses in the Exodus such deep concern. It is this all- consuming love of gold in the church's wealthy laity and her richly beneficed clergy that makes them competitors with the promoters of " blue back,' and to appear to the puLlic eye as all the more sordid and mean. If the people I are to imbibe their morals from the church, as we are told they have hitherto done, then we need not wonder at the tenacity, the love for gaming and ticket-buying, with all I its evils, has on them. If the church is to teach morals, ' let her be consistent and practice her dwn injunctions. Let her, when enjoining the people to faithfully observe the laws, take the lessons Id herself, and not to make the statutes "more honoured in the breach than in the obser- vance."—Yours, dec., IV. IVO GAN. I

div.head: "CLIFFORD DIX'S" REJOINDER. .
div.p: "CLIFFORD DIX'S" REJOINDER. .

Sir,—Although in his discursiv;-17e-jO'inde-r-1; my last letter "Clifford Dix touches upon almost "everything by turn Fend nothing long," there i 3 just one point in it which I should like to notice. He says he is not to be frightened Out of his free trade opinions by the speculations of "Civia." This is an unfortunate phrase for "Clifford Dix" to use. For what did I say ? I merely said that the foreign protective powers would neutralise any reduction in freight- age which English manufacturers might gain by the Ship Canal by simply raising their tariffs. This is something more than a speculatbn ; it is ahnost a certainty. Foreign posers protect their own manufacturers by tariffs against any advantage which English manufacturers may have, and it is not for a moment doubtful that any additional advan- tage the latter may gain will be counteracted by an increase ; of tariffs. That thenfare tariffs is certain, and that if Eng- lith manufacturers were by any means enabled to compete i successfully with their protected rivals these tariffs would be raised is almost equally certain. Yet "Clifford Dix" seems to think that if he recognises these facts he must give up his free trade opinions. His belief in free trade is clearly badly based, and is not held as beliefs of that kind sua•ht to be held. He holds_his belief in free trade in the I,

ante way as the benighted African fetish-worshipper holds hie----by the tenacious grip of fanaticism; and he is equally determined "not to be frightened out of it." "Clifford Dix" may perhaps be surprised to learn that I ant as faithful a believer in free trade as he is himself. But Ide not believe in it because I shut my eyes to palpable facto, but because I believe it to be a scientific truth capable of scientific demonstration. Whilst believing in free trade, I cannot admit that it really exists except as between Eng- land and her dependencies, and a few foreign nations who are not " enlightened " enough to trouble themselves about economic doctrines, true or false. "To buy in the cheapest market and to sell in the dearest" is the popular formula of free trade, but where do we fimi the conditions of this formula fulfilled except in the few instances I have mentioned. To buy in the cheapest market is not free trade, nor yet is it free trade to sell in the dearest. The two must be combined, and if we are only permitted te buy in the cheapest market, and not to sell in the dearest the whole thing is dislocated and out of joint. For the Balla of illustrating this point, let us suppose that a physiological truth was formulated is the words " Plain food is best when the constitution is sound." It is clear that in acting upen this formula we must have all its essen- tia! conditions. It would be foolish if, upon the strength of it, an inelvidual with a disordered constitution were to pereist in taking plain foot It would be wiser in him to take medicine and to adopt a corrective regimen which, though injurious if his constitution were eonnd, is now neceesary in order to escape worse evils. So with free trade. When it exists the commercial constitution is sound, and it deserves all the paneygrics which "Clifford Dix" can be- stow upon it. But when one of the essential conditions of free trade in wanting, Ills absurd te talk and to act as if it existed in its entirety. Another condition of things has then arisen, and a new treatment is required. What this new treatment ought to be is a separate and most difficult inquiry. Some politicians who are out of office and wish to be in say that the new treatment ought to consist of retaliatory tariffs. They may or may not be Correct, bet their motives are such that their suggestions should be regarded with suspicion. Others say a Royal Commission will point a way out of the difficulty. I agree with "Clifford Dix" in condemning this proposal. What is wanted is the discovery or the defining of the economic laws which govern the phenomena of the case in question. There is no royal road to this knowledge neither by com- mission nor otherwise. Such things have always hitherto been done by individual men of genius, and Royal Com- missioners are not now likely to develop a faculty for doing what they have never yet done. There being therefore so many difficulties in the way of applying a remedy, and the danger being so great that the remedy may prove to be worse than the disease it seems to me that it would be very on. wisa to interfere hastily with our preseet commercial svetem. But, the ardent advocates of protection and other similar panaceas may say, work is scarce and becoming scarcer, and the working classes are already beginnisg to keenly feel the pangs of the distress which waits on bad trifles. To thie I would reply that protection at the beet is a very doubtful remedy, and may very likely make thiegs worse, and besides there are other and surer ways by which the dietresees of the working classes may be relieved. There is ample scope for fruitful inquiry into the reasons why, alt'tough labour is ever becoming, throagh invention and science, more productive than it used to be, an ever lessen- ing proportion of its produce goes to the producers. And. again, I would join with "Clifford Dix" in inviting these disinterested friends of the working-man to consider the land question and to try to bring to an end the present system of land-holding, which is nothing but a gigantic monopoly, and which like all monopolies, though it leads to the aggrandiser ent of the monopolists, impoverishes the rest of the community, and above all, robs the toiler of the fruits of hie toil.—l am, sir, CIVIS.

div.head: HIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1984
div.p: HIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 13, 1984

REDUCTION OF RENTS. Sir,—lf there is not quickly some advance in the present low price of wheat, our egricultural population will be knocking at the landlord's door for are luction of rent. As soon as the land upon the GI idstone, Derby, Westminster, and other estates is forced down be, per acre, these indi- viduals will inquire why the need for this reduction exists? If, also, one landlord is to suffer, why should not another landlord—the house landlord disgorge something ?' Ile, too, walks about in idleness, whereas a reduction in house rent would perhaps give greater relief to the greatest number than any other single means that could be adopted. As house rents have been much advanced during past years, there is no real reason why landlords should not feel the pinch of depression as well as other classes.—Yours truly, TOWN 'l ENANT.

needs a little thought to be all brushed away. "Foreign ! governments grant SUM of money to steamship companies to run at low freights ; if we do not act as others do, bow can we succeed ?" There is a charming simplicity in this remark of your correspondent. He only needs to work the problem out for himself and he will see, first, that the Go- vernment pay their subsidies out of moneys raised by tax- ing the people, and next, that the whole of the people are 1 'poor in consequence of such taxation, and that the ooly pitties profiting by the subsidies are the actual receivers of the money. Of course, this answer does not suit the Fair Trader. "Why not," he says, "throw out a sprat to catch a whale?' Well. I answer simply because you would have to throw out no many sprats that your whale when caught would do you no good. If foreign wire should be tamed, why not foreign leather ? If you tax these, why not tax corn, and so on, until everything we consume would be taxed ? An increase of wages would be necessary, and es we should end in increasing the cost of production instead of lowering it. . _

Warrington, December 10, 1884. A LIVERPOOL TORY LEADER ON "FAIR TRADE." Sir,—Sir W. B. Forwood, one of the ablest and most ex- perienced of the citizeus of Liverpool, and a man whose commercial status is certainly of the highest character, and whose position as a local Tory leader, I suppose, is well known, delivered a speech on Saturday evening last to an audience of Liverpool working-men which deserves special notice at the present time. When we find so many of the leaders of the Tory party in the country sacrificing their conscientious convictions and remaining silent, while mem- berm of their party of less influence and character are openly propagating doctrines which, if again adopted into our fiscal system, can only breed irreparable disaster to the toiling millions of our countrymen, it is certainly refreshing indeed to meet with "one righteous man' who sets "country " above mere party interest, and does not hesitate to condemn proposals which his personal experience and knowledge prove to be as dangerous as they are false If Mr. Lawrenson, and those who think with him, would take the advice given by Sir Willem at the end of his speech— an extract from which follows—viz, take a six months' trip to America, I have little doubt that if it is possible Input wisdom iota their heads without resorting to that surgical operation which is occasionally successful in preventing men from going "soft," they would come back free from the heresy of Fair Trade. There is abundance in it to keep tho fair sex on the tip-toe of interest, if not excitement. Tee large extra-coloured ; plate for Christmas' with the title of "A Tiff," is a copy of an oil painting by Messrs. Laslett and Pott. It represents la young couple, in the dress of a bye-gone generation, who have "had words," and have turned thine backs on each I other. It is a really be aitiful picture. We have also to ' hand from the same publlhers (Messrs. Goubaud and Son) i" Le Moniteur de la Mode," with four coloured plates, and ' the usual illustratiors and reviews; and " Myres Three- penny Journal." "The Season" (Is.) maintains its popu- larity as a fashion book and lady's illustrated magazine. Its coloured plates are very highly finished. . " Cassell's Magazine " for December, which is the first issue of a new volume, is exceptionally attractive. The frontispiece illustrative of the verse "Coming through the wood," is very pretty, and the other illustrations are more than usually good. Two new stories are commenced—" A Diamond in the rough," and "Sweet Christabel ;" and there are severalenteresting sketches, including "Sir Julius Bene- dict," "The Metropolis of Shrimps," "Railway Travelling in Comfort and safety," and "A Shilling a day and his Board." "Our Model Reading Club' is a new feature which is likely to prove very valuable. The current number of " The Quivee " well sustains its claims to supply "Sun- day and general reading," " Mollie's Maidens" and "A Poor Man's Wife" are now well on their way. "A Bit of Blue Ribbon "will charm temperance readers; it is a touch- ing story, and is nicely illustrated. The Bishop of Edin- burgh gives the first of two chapters on "The Mysteries of Revelation and of Nature ;" there is some good verse, and the "Short Arrows" continue to reach their mark. "A ' Helping Hand " is the title of a striking frontispiece to. "Little Folks." "A Little too Clever" is brought to a close, but there is to be a new story—" Not Found Out," by the SAMS author. " Going to sea in a cage," an old sailor's story, win please big as well as little folk. The twentieth volume is concluded with this month's part, but there are good things in store for the coming year. There will be an attrac:ive coloured picture with the January part, entitled "Three Little Kittens.' Part four of the fine art edition of LongfAlow's Poetical Works leads off with a beautiful full page engraving ef "A street in Madrid," an illustra- tion of " the Spanish Student." The drama, which is admirably illustrated, is finished in the present number, and we have the commencement of "The Belfry of Bruges " and other poems. Part 11. of " Cassell's Encyclopcedic Dictionary " continues with the letter IL The words " Braema " and " Brahamanism" occupy between them close upon a page; and under these heads the ordinary reader will get all he warts to know as to the system of re- ligious belief and practice of the Brahmans. We mention this by way of illustration of the far-reaching nature of this great work. "The Book of Health' (part 8) deals with c.ffee, cocoa, chocolate, beef-tea, dm, as stimulants ; and opens an important section on "Education and the Nervous System," by Dr. J. Chricton Browne. Pare its anxious as to the schoonlife of their children will study with special interest the large body of facts which are herein brought before them, "Popular Gardening" is varied as ever as to contents, and bright with illustrations. " Ferns" is continued, and there is an introductory ar- ticle on the decorative use of flowers, besides papers on florists' flowers, orchids, the rose and its culture, the vine and its fruit, dec. "The English Illustrated Migazine " is a wonderful shilling's worth, being a "Christmas double number." The frontispiece is a charming "Study for the picture of King Copheata and the Beggar Maid," from a drawing by E. Burne Jones. " Feeding the pigeons" is another noteworthy full page engraving. There is an article in " Clovelly "by Mr. F. Pollock delightfully illustrated by Mr. L. R. O'Brien. Thomas Gainsborougb, R. A.," is dealt with by Mr. Comyns Carr, and Mr. A. Forbes is to the fore amongst the lighter papers with "A Christmastide in the Khyber Pass." " Cape Cod Folks," by Sally Pratt McLean. is a shilling one volume novel issued by Messrs Griffith, Ferran, Okeden, and Welsh. It is racily written, and although it cannot be acid to take high rank as a story, the reader will find his interest in the sayings and doings of the simple fisher folk well suetaiued. Some of the cbaracters are drawn with a clearness and vigour indicative of real power. Grandma and Grandpa Keeler are limned with a loving hand; and the climax is finely reached in the "Death of the Cradlebow." The humour of the work is thoroughly American in its flavour. "The Technical Journal and illustrated Sal f-instructor " is a new publication which is being issued by Messrs. Ward, Lock, and Co. Part Ito hind (price 01) is very promising. It is large in size, there is an abundance of letter press, and the paper is of good quality and high finish. It is accom. ,nan:ed by a folding supplement which comprises about 50 types of different styles of domestic architecture. In ad- dition to drawings and diagrams there is to be a cyclopedic dictionery of terms in science and industrial art. "The Technical Journal" comes out in the nick of time, seeing that the attention of the public is being more and mare directed to the necessity of technical education.

I Take th-e cue article of all others that needs no artificial protection—ceal ; Nature protects this for us. Yet what is the position of coal owner and collier? Do they differ from other branchee of commerce? Not a bit. Colliers' wages go up and down ; coal owners become bankrupt just as in other trades, and yet though everyone is agreed that colliers deserve high wages to compensate for the extra risk, they are amongst the lowest of the wage-earning elaeses. The economic position of Fair Traders is narrow. Like " Fair Price," they are content with saying " wheat is cheap, still trade is bad.'" They never ask themselves the question how we should be placed, supposing wheat was dear, and their crotched failed to make trade good. Yes, I refer to the land qlestion, because I consider it the corner stone of the miserable edifice we have erected, and that we are satisfied to call our " social system." Work- ing-men may combine to resist capital, they may in their meetings continue to denounce employers for reducing wages. More than this, they in aY denounce, as they always do, in all trades, their leaders who dare to give them honest advice. It will all end in their continued state of subjection. Every public speaker, and every capable writer during the past decade has urged upon working-men the extreme urgency of their at once honestly and frankly stating their willingness to do all that can be done, to ask employers to meet them with a liberality of payment that should encourage alike willingness on the port of the employe. Until this is done we shall be compelled by the very nature of things to come down to the lowest paid of Continental workmen. Placing tariffs on imported goods will not help Us. The whole social system is rotten to the core; rich men get richer, and the only satisfaction there is is that they are increasing more and more. Let working-men at once throw overboard party politics; form a People's Party; sends sufficient number of their own class to Parliament to infinence legislation. Then they may hope for something better; they cannot possibly expect rich men will legisla'ithe power out of their own hands. CLIFFORD DIX.
CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE
SOCIETY.

1 and 2 :—The Engineer submitted statements showing the cost of the work from the river to Simm's Crofs, and com- paring the cost with the amounts of the tenders, which show that the two contracts have been completed for £2,500 14s 8d less than the tenders. The committee consider this very satisfactory and highly creditable to Mr. Copland.— The Chairman in moving the confirmation of these minutes gave a detailed statement as to the cuntracte, and concluded by saying that they would see that the committee had con- sidered the statement with regard to the contracts as satis- factory and highly creditable to Mr. Copland. He thought if the Board would confirm that, they would be aoing what was just to Mr. Copland, and they might express a desire that he might have success in his future career, or somethin to that effect.—Mr. Webster seconded the confirmation of:the minutes.—Mr. Wright said he did not see anything grand in the report or anything for which they need eulogise the engineer. He should like to know hew all the disasters came about. It the engineer had used his skill and judg- ment as an engineer ought to have done they would very likely not have had the present collapse. He thought the saving referred to in the minutes were owing to over-estimat- ing the cost in the first instance.—After seine further die- cussion, it was resolvea to confirm the minutes as proposed by the coonnittee.

The annual meeting of the Warrington branch of this society took place in the Public H,ll, on Monday evening, when the chair was occupied by the Mayor (Alderman liar- rieon). He was supported by the follo,eing gentlemen : Revs. J. Barbridge (Everton), J. H. Acheson (Chester), E. C. E. Carleton, T. P. Kiikham, J. Philips, J. G. Richards, W. R. Montgomery, J. Weller, C. C. Harrison, G. Allton, J. Williams, and J. first (diocesan secretary) • Mr. E. P. Parry (Liverpool), deputation ; and Messrs. W. Bea- mont, Dr. Mackie, J. Fairclough,J.P., W. J. Burgess, R. A. Naylor, C. S. Burgess, and W. Coates.—The MAYOR said that during the last twelve months the society had been cluing diligently the good work that it had set itself to do, and had been endeavouring to make the drunkard sober and show him how to make his home bright and cheerful. Fresh branches bad been opened in various localities, and eff Jrte had been successfully made to mitigate the sufferings of some of our unfortunate fellow-creatures who were cons' antly going in sad coming out of prison, and in many cases they had been per- suaded to abandon intemp2rance. During the year 60,000 tracts, pledgehoJks, badges, cards, Jrc., lied boen issued, the receipts fa. which amounted to £ll9 3s 3d. He thought that the cause was rapidly progressing, but was of opinion that its past progress had been greatly retarded by the intemperate language of its advocates of 30 or 40 years ago, when amongst other extravagances it was asserted that a moderate man who never got drunk was worse than a drunkard. He was glad that now, mild, temperate, and kindly language had taken the place of coarse abuse.—Mr. W. J. BURGESS proposed " That this meeting pledges its cordial support in aid of the work of the Diocesan Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society, as in its opinion much of the success that has marked the progress of the temperance movement in the United Kingdom of late years, is due to the ' dual basis' which is the dis- tinguishing characteristie of the Church of England Tem- peranceSocietv." He remarked that the evil of intemperance was not local, but national, and a widespread and national effort such as was made by that society was needed to deal succ-ssfully with it. He commended the Church Temper- ' ance Society to hearty support, and asked them to sink all differenc.s in a holy crusade against drink, the enemy of their race and their religion. (Cheers.)—The Rev. JOHN BURBRIDGE seconded the resolution remarking that the society's chief weapon was the gospel. They believed in the usefulness of the pledge under certain circumstances, but looked upon is as liitle value unless the spirit of tied changed the hearts of the intemperate.—Dr. Macxix supported the retolution, which was carried with applause.— The Rev. S. WILKINSON proposed "That this meeting, hav- ing regard to the fact that intemperance is widely spread and is the source of moral degradation, poverty, and crime, pledges itself to support all means used for the suppression of this vice, and ventures to express the hope the magis- trates and others charged with the administration of the law will exercise their powers ia restric jog the numbers of licensed houses, and in taking such other measures as will lessen the temptation to which our fellow-countrymen are exposed."—The resolution was seconded by Mr. E. P. Perna, and carried unanimously.—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.
WIDNES. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

It would be ungracious on the part of the Board if they did not meet the offer, and he proposed that tho clerk be in- ' structed to write that they would supply the water subject 1 to the fittings being tone satisfaction of the gas and water 1 engineer.--Mr. Forster secOrlded this proposal, which was 1 earned unanimously. ' WIDNES AND THE REDISTRIBUTION OV SEATS —The Chairman said the clerk suggested that it fell withi-r the province of Widnes Local Board to do what might be necessary if anything was necesSary to ensure that Widnes should ke the centre of a district which will be defined under the new Redistribution of Seats Bill. It might be worth while for the B, ,rd to formulate a resolation and send it to Sir Char.(' Mike on the subject. He did not know that being the centre of a district or a divi- sion would do Widnes any immediate good frem a financial point of view, but it would perhms add to the prestige and impsrtance of the place. The following re-olution had been 1 drawn up:—" That this Board desir, • respectfully to draw the attention of the president of tbe Local Goverantent Board to the claim of Widnei, to be r• stunted the centre of that division of the county of Lance -r in which it will be placed when the R distribution of Seats Bill bzcomes law, and to express a hope that when the time comes for defin- ing and naming the a id division due weight will I, given to the said claim. And th t the clerk to th's Beard t : directed to forward a copy of this r elution to Sir Charles Dilke and to inform him as to the population, rateable value, dm., of the township of Widnes." He (the chairman), pro- posed this resolution.-. Mr. Handley seconded it, with , le addition that the General Purposes Committee be instructed to press the claims of Widnes on the Boundary Commis- sioners.—Mr. Webster thought they wanted something else in Widnes besides being the centre of a district—they wanted the Ballot Act. That would be of more benefit to them, and he proposed that they have the Ballot Act as well.—The Chairman thought they could not mix up the two subjects.—Mr. IYebster said he didn't know but what it would be better to go in for having a borough.—The Clerk pointed out that they would not get a member et their own on that account. —The chairrnan s resolution was then car- ried, after which Mr. Handley moved that the General Pur- poses Committee ba instructed to take what action they thought proper before the Boundary Commissioners.—This propord was also carried.

THE HOSPITAL.—The confirmation of the minutes of the Hospital Committee, which contained nothing of impor- tance, was moved by Mr. Sadler, and seconded by Mr. Martley.—Mr. Midwood asked if it was a fact that patients had been brought to the hospital from other districle and kept there at the ordinary rates thiy charged for Widnes people.--Mr. Sadler : There was one case of that kind, that of a farm labourer, who had been sent in by Dr. Cooper without any authority.—The Chairman : It would be a mistake, and would not occur again, I suppose.—Mr. Sadler said the man would be brought up again at their next meet- ing.—The minutes were then confirmed. SEWERAGE COMMITTEE,—This Committee's minutes con- tained the engineer's report, from which we give the fol- fowing extracts :—" Contract No. 2:—The work of this contract was completed on the 27th ult. ORI FOR THE UNEMPLOYED. Mr. Wright suggested that at the prose/it time when there were many able-bodied men unemployed in Widnes, the Board should provide some extraordinary work. He should like to see either the High- way Committee or the whole Board take the matter up.— The Chairman said he was not aware that there were many people out of work; there were none of the works at a standstill, he believed. BANK STREET.—Mr. Midwood said the chairman and he, who were appointed as deputation, had met the Messrs Bol- ton with regard to Bank-street, and the chairman told them that the Board could not authorise them to close the street, for. power to do which they would have to apply to magis- trates. He believed that Messrs Bolton were now tak- ing action for applying to quarter sessions for the clos- ing of the street.—Dr. O'Keeffe proposeA that the Highway Committee be instructed to take steps to oppose the appli- cation of Messrs Bolton.—Mr. Dutton seconded tbis pro- posal which was carried. div.head: AN ARTIST AT WORK, AND lIIS GIFT
div.p: AN ARTIST AT WORK, AND lIIS GIFT
TO THE INFIRUARY.

On Thursday evening Mr. George Sheffield, the artist, executed a drawing in black and white for the benefit of the Warrington Infirmary under condi- tions which, we believe, have not been paralleled except by himself. It appears that some twelve or fourteen months ago he promised Mr. B. Rudge, secretary to to the Working-men's Infirmary Com- mittee, to furnish him with a picture, the proceeds of which should be given to the Institution; but Mr. Sheffield is something of a Bohemian—he is here. there, and everywhere in the course of a year—and there was no thought of tying him to time. Seeing him in Warrington on Wednesday evening, Mr. Thos. Morris reminded him of his promise, upon which the artist said he was ready to fulfil his engagement. It seems that it was part of the bargain that the draw- ing should be begun and finished at a sitting at Mr. Morris's house, the artist stipulating that Mr. Badge and other foremen employed at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' Iron Works should be present to witness the performance as a lesson to them in art. Accord- ingly on Thursday evening there was a goodly as- sembly under the roof of Mr. Morris, a number of personal friends having also been invited to be present. Mr. Sheffield attended, accompanied by Mrs. Sheffield, and Mr. 'dirties, photographer, who had seen to a virgin sheet of paper 3ft. 3in. by 2ft. 3in. being suitably mounted. The artist commenced his task soon after half-past eight, rubbing on charcoal with a freedom which suggested to the un- initiated that it could not possibly result in anything pietwesque. But by-and-by heavy smears began to take the form of light clouds, and with a magic twirl of the fingers, a sun was created which suddenly li-sht A up the dark scene. Order was evolved out of chaos, for presently a particularly black patch resolved itself into the hull of a ship ; masts shot into the air before the astonished g iz,3r could say " Tack Robinson," and presently a noble vessel was seen calmly resting on the calm waters. Again the magic fingers moved, and presently a sloop came into sight, along with other small craft. For the first time it was seen that there was a large buoy in the foreground, whilst right away in the distance, as far as the eye could reach, were "ships of many nations" like many specks on the ocean. It was morning light ; the mist was fleeing before the rising sun ; sea gulls were careering near the masts of the " tall admiral ;" and one winged creature looked strangely dark in the stream of light in whiffi it was floating with out-stretched wings. It was sunrise over the sea, the beginning of a new day, and the end of a new work of art a picture,—the like of which could be produced under such con- ditions by Mr. George Sheffield only. The ar- tist, we may add, worked leisurely ; he was not in one of his most rapid moods, and yet he was rapid, for the picture was begun and finished in less than two hours. ft seemed to maker no difference to him that the company were laughing and talking, and enjoying the hospitality of the genial host, whilst he was lasTa at work. He kept on and on, malring no pause except to straighten hie back or , take a pull at the cigar which dueing the Drat hour I was never out of his left hand. The result was a highly finished drawing of great power and beauty, and of such value intrinsically that it will, we are sure, be the means of bringing a respectable sum to the Infirmary. It was arranged that Mr. Dirties should see to its being at once suitably framed, after which it will be publicly exhibited, and sold on its merits. On the motion of Mr. Rudge, seconded by Mr. J. Walker, a most cordial vote of thanks was tendered to Mr. Sheffield for his handsome gift, and Thompson, who supported it, spoke as a teacher' of art in terms of high praise of the merits of the ' picture—of its power as a specimen of l'ght and shade, of the fine gradation of tone, of the sympathy which it revealed with nature—all giving tokens of the work of a man of genius. Mn, Sheffield suitably replied, remarking that what he could do was little as compared with what he felt might be done. Art had made great strides in his time, and he believed it was making stiff greater. He was glad to have kept his word, and to find that they were pleased with the picture- Several gentlemen present expressed them- selves as delighted with the rare treat which had been afforded them, and thanks were tendered to Mr. and Mrs. Morris for their hospitality on the occasion.

Tbe Empr.ss Eugenie left Windsor Castle on Friday morning, on the cmclusion of her visit to the Queen. Mr. David Davies, M.P., has contributed a donation of £l,OOO to the Welsh Calvinistic Methodist Ministers' Fund.
It is authoritatively aucounced that Sir Stafford North- cote is prepared to contest the fiarnstaple Division of Devon- shire.

Mr. Pelham, boundary commissioner, held an inquiry at Taunton, yesterday, relative to the proposed division of Somersetshire, under the Redistribution of seats Bill. Up to noon yesterday the two prisoners convicted of murder in connection with the Mignonette case had re- ceived no intimation respecting either their sentence or pardon._
The Connt,ss of Breadalbane hag fo,•warded fifty pairs of blanket& to be distributed amongst the Dundee unemployed, and has agreed to sing at the concert in their behali next Monday.
