hum lAnotnEßS' DWELLINGS.—The report of the Select Committee on Irish labourers' dwellings, issued on Friday, recommends that Boards of Guardians should have pewer to acqnire half-an-acre of land for cottages where prac- ticable, and ba compelled to abolish uninhabitable dwel- lings.

ilontEs OF Two CHILDREN FOI7NDs- An extraordinary discovery was made in Glasgow on Thursday night. The bodies of two children were found wrapped in a newspaper on the top of the wall which encloses the Southern Necro- polis. Medical opinion is to the effect that the children were twins and were prematurely born. The police have no clue to the mother.

CIVIL SERVICE. REGULATION.—Friday night's Gacetfr! publishes a Privy Council order extending to the whole of the permanent civil service the regulation recently enforced in the Treasury Department requiting a civil servant seek- ing a seat in the House of Commons to resign his office as soon as be issues his address to the electors or in any other manner announces himself a candidate. A SUICIDAL FAMILY.—At ten o'clock on Friday morning a fire tenter named Samuel Fitton committed suicide by hanging himself by his scarf to a nail in the cellar of his sister's house, George-street, Bury. His mother, 20, years ago, cut her throat, and his brother hung himself four years ago at Rochdale. The deceased had been suffering from pleurisy, and had been lotv spirited for some time.

ANOTHER PRIZEFIGHT —On Friday morning another desperate prizt for £2O took place in Birmingham' be- tween Jim Lane, son of the famous pugilist Hammer Lane, and Withers, of Walsall. The fight lasted without interrup- tion for an hour and twenty minutes, when Lane had his man beaten, and knocked him out of time. Withers waq fearfully punished, and was knocked down several times. BRUTAL MURDER OF AN OLD Marc. On THRSCIay night, at Itanzarugh, near Coartmackherry, an old man

named John Murphy, was murdered in his own house, fear- tul injuries having been inflicted on him by a spade. His son-in-law. Jeremiah Mtlarthy, who lived in the house, has been arested and charged with the murder. The deceased and the prisoner had had violent disputes respecting the farm. SUPPOSED SUICIDE AT HEYWOOD.—On Friday, morning the body of a married woman named Mary Opensbaw, aged 37, of Todd-street, Heywood, was found in a mill lodge in Bury-road, Heywood. The deceased had been in a low state of mind since her confinement, about a month ago. She was, up to a day or two ago, visited by Dr. Jameson. She left her home during the night time. Her husband works at Ashton. THE HARRISON-PAGE DIVORCE SUIT—The ninth day's hearing of the C 155 Harrison v. Harrison and Page, in which the plaintiff sued for a divorce on the ground of his wife's adultery with the co-respondent, Dr. Page, concluded ,on Friday, before Mr. Justice Butt and a special jury. His Lordship, in summing up, said he did not think either of the three partiee most interested were entitled to much sym- pathy, as their conduct had been such as to disentitle them to consideration at the hands of a jury. After a prolonged absence the jury were unable to agree, and were dis- charged. MURDER ny Folsom/ea.—The inquest on the body of Mrs. Matilda Hicks, widow, residing at Lympsham, Somer- setshire, who 'wee supposed to have been poisoned by her nephew, John Frost Day, assisted by Miss Tallard, gover- ness, was resumed at Lympslemn on Friday. Mr. Steven- son, official ,analyst from London. and otter experts, deposed to finding strychnine in the deceased's stomach,*anci in the remains of the gruel of which she had partaken at Dav'S eolicitation. The jury, after 20 minutes' consulta- tion, returned a verdict of wilful murder against Day, but entirely exonerated Miss Tallard, who has also been in custody. MRS Wetmore —The hearing of the action brought by Mrs. Weldon to recover £lO,OOO from Mr. Riviere as damages for an alleged assault in ejecting her from Covent Garden Theatre, on the 29th October and 6th November, 1879, was concluded on Friday. The jury, after long de- liberation, found that defendant was not legally in posses- sion on the occasions when the assaults were committed, and, as upon this finding defendant had no rigbt to eject the plaintiff, the judge entered a verdict for the plaintiff and asked the jury to assess damages. The jury were unable to agree upon this point, and ultimately were discharged, and verdict and judgment were entered for the plaintiff without damages. The judge awarded Mrs. Weldon £5O for costs. ALLEGED CONSPIRACY TO MURDER A CHILD.—The Cam. berwell police were recently made acquainted by a man named Barnard that he had been offered £lO to drown a child. They allowed him to proceed with those who made the offer, and on Thursday evening they saw the child handed to him, with the sum named. They immediately arrested two men and a woman. The child is a girl, and a fortnight old.—At the Lambeth Police Court, Thomas Long, 42, painter, Camberwell; George Fletcher Walker. 27. land agent, Camberwell; and Kate Day, 27, draper, Champion Hill, were charged with conspiring to murder a female child at Burton-road, Camberwell, on Thursday night. The police officers secreted themselves behind a fence and watched Barnard meet the prisoner Day, who carried a baby which she handed to Barnard, and returned the way she came. Witness followed and arrested her, and Walker coming up, he was also arrested. On arrival at the station Barnard handed witnese a small bag containing ten sovereigns. Hay declared that she was not guilty. Long said the child was given to Btrnard to adopt; Walker said nothing. The prisoners were remanded.

PARIS FRIDAY AFrErtwoow.—Tt is officially announced from Madagascar via Zanzlhar that the French have cap- tured the forts South of Kobemar, killing two hundred Hovas and capturing five guns. THE CHOLERA. MADRID FRlDiv.—During the last twenty-four hours one death from cho!era and one case are announced from Toledo. No further cases are reportad from Yerrgel, in the province of Alicinte.

div.head: FAIR TRADE.
div.p: FAIR TRADE.
Sir,—Pray do not g-ra—m-h-le-iii;k for a little of your space in which to say a few mora words respecting this Ghost of the Past.

_ I often ask myself of what Ll3O are all the histories that are piled upon the bookshelves of our public libraries. Do our working-men 'read them? Do they really learn any- thing from them ? _One would think that if the lives of our • .

great men were stud'ed as they ought to be we should not have such wild, such chimerical crotchets trotted out for our acceptance as this of Fair Trade. What argument will con- vince the Protectionist that he is following a will-e'-the- wisp ; that like the unwary tsaveller, he wilt most certainly flounder and flounder until all poseibility of gaining solid ground is gone for ever. I beg that these Fair Traders will spend a few hours in Bold-street studying the lives of John Bright, of Cobden, of Sir Robert Peel. Read of the harrowing scenes that met the gaze of these reformers in the days when the Repeal of the Corn Laws was the object striven for. Read the stirring incidents that were the every day life of the poor of our large towns in Lancashire and Yorkshire ; how everything that came into the poor man's house was taxed. From the cradle to the grave the tax- gatherer was the millstone that hung round the neck of the people. There was no competition in those days. Eagland , was the workshop of the world, and yet what was the state 1 other people ? Without public libraries, without public , I parks, with combination laws in existence, the working- 1 man was crippled in opportunities for educating himself and crippled in his action through life. True, in those days ' I bright flashes of native intelligence made themselves ap- parent. The inventive mind of some of our brightest geniuses stood out in bold relief from the ranks, and a ' Stephenson and a Watts made it possible for their succes- sors to alter things; but what was the condition of the I general public forty years ago ? I have no wish to deal with the two classes, workmen and employers, separately. I Less than forty years ago all the wire manufactured at Ilvlands's could be knocked about in a hand-cart, the "Brothers" themselves taking an active part in the draw- ing process. What a wonderful alteration has come about since then. Nay, within the last twenty years what an al- teration. Employers have become ounty magnates, and workmen in all trades are in receipt of higher wages by a considerable amount. And still we have people so blinded to the experience of the past that they wish to return to it. What especial interest shall we select for protection ? Mr. Lawrence, with one of the most rlausible pens ever wielded by a protectionist, cries out "Tax German wire," and what then, may! ask? Shall we then be enabled to manufecture Wire any cheaper than we do now? Oh, no, he will answer, but if German wire is kept out of England the cable companies and the wire weaving firms would have to buy English wire. Would they ? I have a notion it would be like the old saying, " You may take the horse to the water, but you can't make him drink." Nor could you make the foreign customers buy; you would simply do what Sir Stafford Northcote in his admirable letter to Mr. G. Potter says you must not do. With your permission, I will quote from Sir Stafford's letter. It contains several points inter- esting to wiredrawers, and other workmen in the town : " Sometimes we find ourselves face to face with impedi- ments which are absolutely insuperable, and which it is but waste of time and strength to contend against; but more commonly, I think there are remedies to be found in the ex- ercise of greater skill." I suggest that Fair Traders who are simply designing to support the Conservatives, thinking that party will return, even by the merest shad- to Protec- tion, read the above lines with care and attention. They will perceive there is not a vestige of an inkling towards any desire to return to Protection. As if to answer specially those who would keep out foreign goods by taxation, he says—" We have some advantages which we must take care not to throw away, for they would not be easy to regain. One is our large capital take care not to frighten that away; another is what is called our connexion '—there is a great dell of trade which comes to our shores because it has been the habit of many countries to treat our market as a convenient centre and place of exchange. It would be a serious loss to the country if we lost that depot trade." Now, sir,! contend the whale thing is there in a nutehfl'. It is a benefit to our country to be made a depot for the world's trade. If you injure this especial and particular feature you drive away capital. Why, Sir Stafford has dealt the heaviest blowito Fair Traders it has been their lot to re- ceive.

Of course, I quite object to this being made a party ques- tion, but what was the situation previous to this important letter from Sir Stafford? The Liberal leaders to a man have definitely pronounced against Fair Trade. The Tory leaders had fenced with it. With a cunning worthy of the party, they hoped to gain a few votes by withholding the whole truth, and it is only now at the bidding of the Stan- dard and the Saturday Review that they return to anything like political honesty. One would think that the writers of such letters as the one signed 'Fair Trade" were labouring under the impres- sion that the foreign workmen occupied a superior position to the English workman. This is all a fallacy, and it only

LIMN. THE BEGGING NIT2EANCE.—At Lynn Police Court, on Thursday, James Gavin, a tramp. was charged before Mr. G. C. Dewhurst with begin g ia the village.—P.C. Bu- chanan proved the case.—Prisoner was seat to prison for seven days, the magistrate remarking that the practise of begging, especially by able-bodied men, must be suppressed. BIBLE ',OCIRTY Menetero.—On Thursday evening a-meet- ing in aid of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Mission Hall, Lymrn, when the chair was taken by the Rev. G. Guest, rector. Thera was a good attendance, amongst those on the platform being the Rev, J. Catlin, of Oughtrington, the Rev. G. S. 6ymons (the deputation),.the Rev, J. W. Kirkland, and Messrs. P, Dutton and D. Boyd. The meeting having been commenced with singing and prayer, the chaiman introduced Mr. Symons, who gave an interesting address on the ramifications of the work done by the society and its great power for good in disieminating religious knowledge. Mr. Kirkland else addressed the meet-. Subsequently a collection, which realised the sum of £3 7a 91, was made, and in addition promises of two sub- scriptions were received. A collection box containing LI. 55 was handed in by Master George Bowen.

IN PARLIAMENT. SESSION 1835. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. WHEREA., a Meeting of the Owners and Ratepayers of tl-e Borough of Warrington, in the Counties of Lancaster and Chester. was held on Thursday. the Twenty-third day of Octo- ber, 1884, in the Public Hall, Rylands-stre,t. in the said Borough, in pursuance of the Act of the 35th and 38th Vic., cap, 91, intituled "An Act to authorize the application of Funds of Municipal Corperations and other governing bodies in certain cases." And whereas at the said Meeting, held at the time and place aforesaid. I, as Chairman of such Meeting, and in compliance with the statute, proposed the following resolution:— " hat this meeting eonsents to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington promoting, in con- junction with others, a local and personal Bill in Parliament for the purpose of ins rporating a Company and empowering such Company to construct a canal from the River Mersey to the City of Manchester, navigable for Ocean Steamers and Ships of large burthen, and to the contribution out of the Borough Rate to the cost of such promotion of a sum not ex- ceeding twopence in the pound upon the annual rateable value of the Borough for one year." And whereas the said resolution, on being put to the Meeting, was carried, whereupon demand was made that such question should be decided by a Poll of the Owztrs and Rate- payers. And whereas a Poll was accordingly taken in manner pro- vided by the Public Health Act, 1875, and the schedules thereto, and the votes recorded thereat were as follows:— In favour of the above resolution Against -- Majority in favour of resolution 5,840 Dated this 3rd esy of December, 1884. JOSEPH HARRISON. Mayor and Returning Officer.

I SHOCK/NO COLLIERY ACCIDENT : FOUR. MEN KILLED.— , Four men were killed on Friday morning in the Navigation , Colliery, Treharris, near Merthyr-Tydvil. The men, it ap- 1 petrs, were repairers, and having finished their night's work, were being raised to the top of the shaft, which Is nearly half a mile deep. When they had ascended a con- siderable distsnce the rope broke, and the cage and its oc- cupants were thrown to the bottom, with the consequence that the men were killed instantaneously. A later telegram says a fifth man had a marvellous es- cape. When the rope bruk3 and the cage com- menced to fall, John Dodd caught hold of the guide . rope and clung thereto. With extraordinary nerve and presence of' mind, be then lowered I,imself 500 yards, until he entangled himself in the wire ropes and guides. ~i• In this position be remained for nearly eight hours, when ,4 his peril was aeoertsined and he was promptly rescued. .q
